The CMS collaboration is utilizing a 1.629 femtosecond precise measurement of the $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ decay to explore rare processes and test the Standard Model's validity. This assessment is based on a 20.8 $\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of 8 TeV proton-proton collisions at CERN, resulting in 137,500 candidates for $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ decays after applying selection criteria. A time-domain fit to $K^+ K^- \mu^+ \mu^-$ final states, considering $J/\psi\rightarrow \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays and different $K^*0$ $K^{\pm}$ decay modes, allows for the extraction of $B^0_s$ meson proper lifetimes and decay width differences, with outcomes of 1.629 $^{+0.005}_{-0.005}$ fs and 0.036 $^{+0.009}_{-0.005}$ ps$^{-1}$, matching previous findings with improved precision. Additionally, yield measurements in different $K^*0 K^{\pm}$ decay modes, along with $m_{K^*K^*}$ distributions in $\rho$ and $\Omega$ channels, are presented with corresponding acceptance and efficiency calculations. These results demonstrate the significance of the LHC in exploring rare processes and testing the Standard Model's limitations. With the full LHC dataset, anticipated improvements of an order of magnitude in rare decay measurements are expected, offering exciting opportunities for discovering new physics phenomena. The CMS collaboration is also working on the $B^0\rightarrow J/\psi K^0_S$ and $L_\mathrm{dir}$ measurements, which feature 1.3 fs and 1.45 fs precision for $B^0$ meson lifetimes, and 1.8 $\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ and 8.8 $\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ datasets for the $B^0\rightarrow J/\psi \phi$ and $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi \phi$ decays, respectively. This study tackles a stochastic control problem with the goal of establishing a
definition of a solution that accounts for the consequences of using a
approximate, or 'discrete,' method to solve the problem. When using this
approximate method, we ensure that our approximation becomes increasingly
precise as we use a finer level of detail. Along with this, we demonstrate the
existence of a solution when the approximate method is used to solve the
problem, and also show that this solution converges to the original problem.
Finally, we end by highlighting the significance of our findings and the
novelty of our approach. One key aspect of our methodology is the introduction
of a new concept known as the "convergence of the approximate control problem
under minimal conditions". This term refers to the idea that our approximate
method produces a solution whose distance from the original solution diminishes
as the level of approximation improves. This achievement is significant because
it allows us to extend the applicability of the stochastic control problem to
scenarios involving 'rough paths', an area previously hindered by the lack of
this convergence guarantee. As a result, we are able to explore the connection
between these 'rough paths' and the control problems mentioned earlier, thereby
establishing a link between two concepts that had no relationship with each
other up until now. This study is an expansion of the findings presented in the
paper "Approximate Optimal Controls in Stochastic Differential Equations" [1]. This research has also led to the creation of two new theorems that are comparable to existing results, as shown in the papers "Approximate Controllability of stochastic Navier-Stokes equations" [2] and "Approximate Optimal Controls in Stochastic Navier-Stokes Equations" [3]. Furthermore, it has provided the foundation for the results presented in the paper "Stochastic Navier-Stokes Equations with Additive White Noise" [4]. The novelty of our approach can be seen in the way we utilize a particular type of approximation method known as the 'numerical method of step size' to achieve the desired level of precision. This approximation method is distinct from other techniques such as the 'finite element method' and the 'boundary element method', which are more traditional in nature. This study can be applied to a broad category of approximation methods, not just the one mentioned above. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays identified through the TA stereo system at the TA observatory in Mexico, revealing a consistent anisotropy pattern, discovered a significant change in anisotropy direction with energy levels above 4 EeV. Our initial study determined that these cosmic rays exhibit anisotropy, with an amplitude of 46 microsteradians at the same energy range, and exhibit a peculiar energy dependence that contradicts the predictions of the "Source and Medium" model. To confirm this finding, we conducted an alternative analysis of our data, employing a dipole component to describe anisotropy patterns, with a calculated amplitude of 41 ± 8 microsteradians for energies above 4 EeV. We further investigated the energy sector immediately below 4 EeV, employing a combined TA and Auger dataset, and found that the anisotropy amplitude exhibited an intriguing energy dependence, with a minimum amplitude occurring at approximately 0.5 EeV, displaying the same characteristics when analyzed with a quadripole component. We also explored other anisotropy patterns, but the results remained consistent with our primary findings. Our study suggests that cosmic rays with energies exceeding 4 EeV exhibit anisotropy characteristics that differ significantly from those with lower energies, and exhibit unique features that require a comprehensive explanation. Our findings pave the way for a re-examination of models that attempt to explain the origins of cosmic rays with such energies. We also emphasize the significance of accurately determining anisotropy patterns in lower energy ranges, and highlight the value of a unified TA and Auger dataset in this context. Our study demonstrates the continued importance of in-depth anisotropy analyses of extremely energetic cosmic rays, and the need for further research into this phenomenon. Our findings are consistent with those of a separate study conducted by the Auger Collaboration, which arrived at the same conclusions with a slightly different methodology. We provide characterizations for the nilpotency and solvability of finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, which are then applied to identify classes of such algebras with specific properties. Our findings also cover the cases of Lie, Leibniz, and Malcev algebras, which can be considered as subclasses of Zinbiel algebras. Our main results are then utilized to examine the properties of these subtypes of algebras, yielding insights into their dimensional requirements and degree rankings. Additionally, our research includes an examination of the conditions under which nilpotent Zinbiel algebras can be characterized by their dimension, as well as an exploration of the relationships between these algebras and their corresponding Lie algebras in the solvable case. Our study also delves into the characteristics of nilpotent Zinbiel algebras with a specific dimension, providing an example of one such algebra and presenting its Lie bracket in a visual format. Our research on these topics is presented through a combination of both theoretical and graphical representations.

This research deals with a newly identified phenomenon called "anisotropic flow fluctuations" that occurs in the high-energy collisions of heavy ions. Unlike "anisotropic flow", which refers to the quirkly moving pattern of particles produced in these events, "anisotropic flow fluctuations" pertain to variations in this pattern from one event to another. A comprehensive statistical model, combined with a theoretical understanding of the quark-gluon plasma that is formed in these collisions, is utilized to interpret the data. The results reveal that the magnitude of these fluctuations are influenced by the characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma and its interactions with the medium it is moving through. Moreover, a new observable that can help pin down the characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma has been proposed. This research also highlights the significance of investigating "knock-out" effects, which arise when a few of the heaviest particles produced in these collisions, known as jets, interact strongly with the surrounding medium, causing it to shift or "knock out" of its equilibrium state. This can, in turn, influence the properties of the quark-gluon plasma and make its study even more intricate. The necessary steps to improve the accuracy of the current understanding of these phenomena are also outlined. The data analyzed in this research is based on the available information from the ALICE, ATLAS, and STAR experiments, which includes a wide range of collision energies and beam projectiles. The theoretical model employed in this research has the capability to interpret not only current but also future data from the ALICE, ATLAS, and CMS experiments, which will allow for further insights into these complex phenomena. This research introduces four-valued logic for answering queries consistently in inconsistent databases. Our approach utilizes Algebraic Model, an algebra-based approach that serves as a foundation for our method. We then introduce four-valued semantics for algebra that facilitates the evaluation of queries on inconsistent databases. This leads to an enhanced algebra that mitigates inconsistencies in databases. We also establish a connection between this algebra and the original databases. Leveraging this connection, we develop algorithms to determine whether a query can be answered consistently and if so, obtain the consistent answer. We also explore extending our solution to address additional issues in databases. This research lays the groundwork for a range of possibilities, including the development of specialized engines for evaluating queries on inconsistent databases, as well as the creation of tools that identify and resolve inconsistencies in databases. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to common database operations and evaluating its performance using actual datasets. This includes the well-known University dataset and the Amazon product dataset. We also examine the generality of our approach by exploring its applicability to other database repair models. This research also touches on the topic of consistent query answering in dynamic databases. This involves determining whether a database change allows for consistent query answering and if so, obtaining that consistent answer. We develop algorithms for this purpose and evaluate the performance of our approach on actual datasets. This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model to analyze non-linear time series dynamics and significant structural changes within count-valued processes. Building on the PARX model, TV-PARX incorporates varying parameters that adapt over time, enabling it to effectively capture changes and complexities within data, even when dynamics are non-linear and the underlying process experiences abrupt shifts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TV-PARX through numerical examples and a real-world application, showing that it yields superior performance when compared with leading alternative methods. Moreover, TV-PARX is capable of accommodating complex dynamics and structural changes without requiring explicit data inputs, differentiating it from other state-of-the-art models. The associated R package allows users to easily utilise TV-PARX in practical settings. Through the analysis of large datasets, TV-PARX offers significant advantages over other models due to its scalable nature. 

With the increasing prevalence of time series exhibiting nonlinear dynamics and abrupt shifts, statistical models are being developed to capture these complex patterns, often employing sophisticated machine learning techniques. These models, while highly effective, come with significant computational requirements, potentially limiting their widespread adoption. To address this issue, this paper develops a time-varying Poisson autoregressive model with exogenous covariates (TV-PARX), a probabilistic model that leverages varying parameters to capture nonlinear dynamics and structural changes without resorting to overfitting. Numerical experiments and a real-world application demonstrate the TV-PARX model's superiority over alternative methods, showcasing its scalable nature due to its implementation using the George-Fossett limited memory algorithm. The TV-PARX model is seamlessly integrated into R via the `tvparx` package, enabling users to effortlessly incorporate the model into their workflow. The growing size of modern datasets necessitates the development of large-scale models, and the TV-PARX model's scalable nature positions it favorably for the analysis of large time series data. The TV-PARX model's ability to capture complex dynamics and structural changes without compromising model interpretability differentiates it from alternative nonlinear time series models, making it a compelling solution for a broad range of applications. This paper introduces Neural Descriptor Fields, a novel framework that
combines a neural network with a descriptive model, thereby enabling the
representation of complex, high-dimensional spaces for various applications.
When applied to the domain of manipulation tasks, such representations can
be viewed as learning important details about an object's physical properties
and its surrounding environment. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this approach
can be employed to perform tasks that require manipulating objects in a
simulated environment, based on a limited number of exemplary demonstrations.
Our proposal is comprised of two primary parts: a learner that utilizes
learning-by-examples to identify key descriptors, along with a generator that
produces actions based on the current situation and the learned descriptors.
This method excels particularly in scenarios with scarce demonstrations,
where it is able to extend its knowledge through trial and error. Our results
show that Neural Descriptor Fields achieve superior performance compared to other
state-of-the-art methods in scenarios with abundant and scarce demonstrations
alike. The underlying technique is then applied to a more intricate task
involving the manipulation of multiple objects in a 3D environment. Our code
is available online at https://github.com/leungwzh/neural-descriptor-fields.

The approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm is a sparse representation technique commonly used to solve synchronization problems, but its convergence near the capacity limit is not well understood. In the AMP context, the equivalence to the replica method's first step leads to the TAP free energy, which is associated with the condensate edge and serves as a baseline for understanding the performance of AMP. To investigate the AMP algorithm's behavior near the capacity limit, we analyzed the TAP free energy's edge behavior in the Z2-synchronization problem and found that AMP's performance plateaus when the gap to capacity is greater than the sample complexity, as predicted by the AMP analysis. To overcome this limitation, we introduced a generalized TAP free energy and showed that its edge behavior determines the performance of AMP in semi-detailed balance when the gap to capacity is less than the sample complexity. To achieve better performance, we designed a two-tier AMP algorithm that matches the performance of the generalized TAP free energy and, as a special case, the condensate edge, thus achieving the optimal sample complexity of N^0.5 for the Z2-synchronization problem. Our proposed algorithm outperformed the standard AMP and the generalized TAP algorithm in simulations conducted on random damped phase transition models. To further analyze the condensate edge, we introduced a new condensate edge theorem for the TAP free energy in the Z2-synchronization context, obtaining more precise information about the edge behavior near capacity limit than previously known. As a related issue, we also investigated the TAP free energy's edge behavior in the random damped Kac-Walker chain model, which provides a more general framework for understanding the condensate edge in the Z2-synchronization context. Our analysis revealed the existence of a condensate edge threshold, below which the TAP free energy's variance increases exponentially with the system size, and our proposed two-tier AMP algorithm's performance plateaus at a certain level near this threshold. Our results also demonstrated the connection between the condensate edge and the AMP algorithm's performance in the Kac-Walker chain context, which is not influenced by the variance of the TAP free energy's edge, and thus has a smoother transition near the threshold. Our research provides a unique perspective on the AMP algorithm's performance near the capacity limit and reveals the crucial role of the condensate edge in understanding the algorithm's behavior. We used wide-field, uncalibrated photometric data from the All-Sky Camera Network at
three different locations in China to estimate the vertical aerosol optical depth
from cloud-free images taken during the summer of 2010. The aerosol optical depth
was determined from the calibration-independent radiance of the Earth's entire
sky, and the resulting values were compared with more precise measurements
obtained using a sun photometer at the China Aerosol Remote Sensing Network
headquarters in Xishuanga. The estimates from the All-Sky Cameras correlated
strongly with the more accurate measurements, yielding a mean difference of
0.33±0.01 per hundred meters, and a standard deviation of 2.56 per hundred meters
for a 95% confidence level. This confirms that wide-field, uncalibrated photometry
can effectively determine the aerosol optical depth in areas with minimal cloud
cover. The resulting data set obtained from the All-Sky Camera Network in China
covers an extensive period and large geographical area, allowing further study
of the spatial and temporal variations of aerosol optical depth in that region. The method employed in this study has the potential to be valuable for other
similar ground-based observation networks worldwide. The data and analysis are
relevant to areas with similar environmental conditions and levels of aerosol
atmospheric pollution. The associated data set has been deposited in the China
National Data Sharing Service, and is also available upon request to the researchers
listed in the 'Contact Persons' section. The data set includes the aerosol optical
depth estimates derived from the All-Sky Camera images at the three locations in
China, as well as the comparison data obtained using a sun photometer at the China
Aerosol Remote Sensing Network headquarters in Xishuanga. The associated software
code is also available online upon request. The code consists of the Python scripts
used to analyze the data and calculate the aerosol optical depth. The code is
primarily based on established methods outlined in reference [22]. The code is

We introduce ProjectSpin, a method for estimating the 3D orientation of general objects within complex real-world scenes. Unlike other pose estimation techniques that consider 3D orientation as a continuous, spherical value, ProjectSpin divides 3D orientation into multiple discrete, non-spherical sections, or "spin-projections." These projections are created by silhouetting virtual 3D objects from multiple synthetic angles, effectively producing 2D images that represent different views of the object. These 2D images are then analyzed using a deep learning technique called a graph convolutional network (GCN), which identifies key projection features and matches them to existing training data, thereby estimating the object's 3D orientation. We demonstrate ProjectSpin's effectiveness by applying it to a challenging outdoor scene retrieval task, in which it achieves superior performance compared to a model considering 3D orientation as a continuous value. We also show that ProjectSpin performs well on a difficult 3D orientation estimation task in 3D point clouds, outperforming baseline models by a significant margin. We highlight the importance of integrating project spin knowledge into the learning process for reliable 3D orientation estimation, and provide comprehensive ablation analyses of ProjectSpin's components. We believe ProjectSpin has the potential to be a valuable 3D orientation representation in various applications, and we encourage the community to explore its capabilities further. We introduce GLRAM, a novel extension to the Graphical Lasso model that enables the estimation of latent structural connections in multivariate Gaussian distributions. The GLRAM model incorporates a second-level graph that represents the relationships between pairs of connected node groups, thereby extending the standard GLM framework. By doing so, we extract a higher-level structure from connected clusters, which can be viewed as a description of the clusters' weights in a collection of sparse, weighted linear combinations. We then develop an algorithm based on the Alternating Direction Method Multiplier (ADMM) to estimate the model parameters, and we establish the consistency of our method under the conditions of cluster identification and irrepresentability. Furthermore, we illustrate the effectiveness of GLRAM through numerical experiments presented in the results section. The code is publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. We also provide a hypothetical scenario to clarify the distinction between GLRAM and other methods for detecting community structures. The name of the paper is "Extended Graphical Lasso for Multivariate Gaussian Distributions with Latent Structures" and it has been published in the journal "Mathematics". This study examines the performance of diverse numerical methods for the Alanine Dipeptide's molecular dynamics simulations using nonlinear differential equations. A wide range of techniques, including traditional molecular dynamics, stochastic differential equations, multi-scale methods, and different numerical schemes was tested to evaluate their computational efficiency and solution accuracy. The most efficient method can be up to 10 times more computationally intensive than the most efficient algorithm tested, yet produces similar results. The study reveals significant discrepancies in both computational time and solution accuracy across various numerical methods for the same level of molecular detail. The most performant algorithms demonstrate a 100-fold decrease in computational time while achieving the same level of accuracy as the most demanding algorithms. The study further divides the numerical methods into two categories based on their accuracy in reproducing kinetic energies and potential energies. The most advanced algorithms show a 10,000-fold difference in computational time for kinetic energies and a 100-fold difference for potential energies when compared to the most precise algorithms. The study suggests that many of the numerical methods tested can be classified as 'fast but inaccurate' or 'accurate but slow'. The most challenging scenario tested required the smallest time step size of 0.001, the largest number of particles of 1000, and the simplest harmonic potential, yet even then showed a wide range of results across the different algorithms, with the fastest one being 8 times faster with a smaller time step size and the most accurate one being 1000 times more precise. The study also examined the performance of the different numerical methods with a larger time step size of 20, a higher number of particles of 5000, and a more complex anharmonic potential, but the overall trends remained similar. The most challenging scenario tested showed a 10,000-fold difference in computational time and a 100-fold difference in precision when using the most accurate algorithm as a reference. The study concludes that even for the simplest biomolecular systems, the choice of numerical method can significantly impact both computational efficiency and solution accuracy. The study further suggests that even for the simplest biomolecular systems like Alanine Dipeptide, the use of advanced numerical methods can provide significant advantages in both computational efficiency and solution accuracy. We examine the impact of inter-layer connections on the distribution of node importance in multilayer networks. Combining centrality measures from different layers can result in varying outcomes, prompting us to investigate methods for calculating combined node importance. However, existing approaches overlook the impact of inter-layer connections on centrality, leading to our identification of three distinct categories based on their influence. We then introduce a new measure, accounting for the effects of inter-layer connections on node importance, specifically in networks with multiple collaborations. Furthermore, we provide a computational framework for calculating our proposed centrality measure, which can be applied to networks without collaborations. Our results demonstrate that inter-layer connections significantly affect node importance and that our proposed measure accurately reflects this effect. We also find that it performs comparably to existing measures, demonstrating the versatility of our approach. We term our measure the Harmonic Centrality Measure (HCM). We then apply HCM to classify influential spreaders in multilayer networks and compare its performance to other centrality measures. Our findings show that HCM effectively identifies the most influential nodes, particularly in networks with collaboration layers. We also make our code publicly available for easy utilization by others. We hope this contribution facilitates further research on the computation of node importance in diverse multilayer network settings. We provide our findings in the following sections. We also provide additional information about our approach and the code we utilized for our study. We hope this information is beneficial for others working in this field. We are confident that our study paves the way for exploring other aspects of node importance in multilayer networks. We believe that our proposed measure, HCM, is a suitable alternative to existing approaches and that our code will be useful for applying our method to various research applications. We analyze the Dirac equation in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, obtaining an explicit representation of the Dirac operator as a combination of the conformal Dirac operator and a scalar operator in the $\kappa$-Minkowski spacetime. This allows us to reduce the Dirac equation in $R$-Minkowski to a system involving a mass term, a conformal parameter, and a differential equation defined within the $\kappa$-Minkowski spacetime. Furthermore, we establish an analogy between solutions to the Dirac equation in $R$-Minkowski and those in de Sitter spacetime, indicating that the latter can be obtained from the former by a conformal transformation. This comparison reveals distinct solution spaces for the Dirac equation in both $R$-Minkowski and de Sitter spacetime. Moreover, we derive the wave equations for scalar fields in both $R$-Minkowski and de Sitter spacetime from their respective mass terms. Finally, we examine the relationship between the solutions to the Dirac equation and those of massless scalar fields in both spacetime geometries. This investigation paves the way for extending the analysis to other relativistic wave equations in $R$-Minkowski and de Sitter spacetime. This research investigated how surface seals behave under various conditions by subjecting a rectangular cavity with a sliding surface seal to different pressures and velocities in computational fluid dynamics simulations. The models accounted for fluid dynamics and the behavior of the surface seal. Results showed that higher impact speeds caused pressure reductions within the cavity and led to the formation of surface waves that could break the surface seal, potentially causing it to slide or become stuck. The speed at which the surface seal stuck increased with outside pressure but was unaffected by the pressure inside the cavity. The CFD models were compared to physical tests with similar results. Changing the shape of the cavity showed that the conditions that led to the surface seal sticking were less likely to occur if the cavity was more pointed. The shapes that did lead to the surface seal sticking were more likely to occur in practice. The conditions that led to the surface seal sticking also led to increased pressure outside the cavity but this had a minimal effect on the surface seal. The pressure outside the cavity was more affected by the velocity at which the surface seal stuck than the pressure inside the cavity. The velocity at which the surface seal stuck increased with the pressure outside the cavity but the relationship was non-linear. The shape of the cavity influenced the pressure outside the cavity more than the pressure inside the cavity. The generalized Witten effect is explored in the context of quantum gravity, referring to the unique physical phenomenon arising from the coupling of a topologically nontrivial gauge field to a gauge invariant action. This phenomenon was initially observed by Edward Witten and has far-reaching implications for the variety of charged states present in quantum gravity. In essence, the generalized Witten effect demonstrates that the coupling of a topologically nontrivial gauge field to a gauge invariant action results in a quantum state that is distinct from all classical charged states. In turn, this leads to a scenario where the spectrum of charged states in quantum gravity remains unbounded, a phenomenon otherwise expected only within the parameters of the parent theory. In this paper, the generalized Witten effect is illustrated through specific examples involving Yang-Mills, Maxwell, and Einstein-Maxwell theories in both two-dimensional spacetime and four-dimensional spacetime. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the effect is not confined to the unbounded spectrum of charged states in quantum gravity but can also lead to the emergence of a continuous spectrum of charged states in quantum scalar field theory and quantum Yang-Mills theory in two-dimensional spacetime. These findings are further reinforced by an in-depth analysis of the Hilbert space of quantum states, which reveals that the coupling of a gauge field to a gauge invariant action results in the creation of a new quantum state located within the causal perturbation theory's physical Hilbert space. This state is characterized by a unique set of properties, including being part of the scattering states, being distinct from all classical charged states, and giving rise to the spectrum of charged states in quantum gravity. In essence, the generalized Witten effect is found to be a fundamental phenomenon of quantum field theory that arises from the interplay between the gauge symmetry, the causality, and the non-trivial topology of the gauge field. It is also shown to be responsible for the boundedness condition of the charge operator in quantum mechanics, which, in turn, ensures that the spectrum of charged states in quantum gravity remains unbounded. In conclusion, this paper delves into the generalized Witten effect through a combination of mathematical proofs and physical interpretations, presenting it as a far-reaching consequence of the coupling of a topologically nontrivial gauge field to a gauge invariant action, which gives rise to the variety of charged states present in quantum gravity. In this study, we propose a novel unet-based model, known as Dilated Dense Attention Unet, and have successfully applied it to automate the detection of esophageal tumors from endoscopic video recordings with ultrasound elastography overlay. The model leverages a combination of dense and attention-based mechanisms to handle the challenges posed by this specific image classification problem. Compared to a standard unet network, the proposed model achieves significant performance enhancements for tumor segmentation tasks. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation metric that considers the accuracy of segmentation in conjunction with the time required to obtain the results. This is particularly relevant because the method we propose has the potential to be used in real-time clinical settings. The proposed model showed an overall improvement of 13.5% in DSC, 17.5% in HA, and 24.8% in ASA scores when compared to the conventional unet network. The results obtained were consistent across repeated experiments and demonstrated the superiority of the proposed model for this specific application. The code for the model has been made publicly available on GitHub. To ensure generalizability, the training dataset was expanded to include multiple institutions. The proposed model shows promise for tumor segmentation tasks and the code is accessible for researchers to test the model on other medical applications. The evaluation protocol used in this study is also applicable to other deep learning-based unet variants. The research is an advancement over previous work that relied on hand-crafted features and did not utilize the ultrasound elastography overlay effectively. The proposed method has the potential for automated precise tumor segmentation in real-time clinical settings, which would be a significant improvement over the current method of outline drawing used by clinicians. The code for the model has been made publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/medison-lab/DDAT_UNET. The research was conducted in accordance with ethical standards and the anonymized data has been made available on Harvard Dataverse at the following link: https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset/api/v2.0/files/5625516. In highly multicultural communities, advanced NLP technologies hold considerable promise, yet integrating them requires addressing significant linguistic barriers. This paper focuses on developing an innovative framework that leverages transfer learning to create a unified, CVC (Core-Vocabulary-Cramming)-based model capable of managing diverse languages. By condensing essential vocabulary into a core component and categorizing the remaining words into crammed layers, this model's structure facilitates effective cross-lingual knowledge sharing while preventing knowledge contamination between crammed layers. As a result, you can obtain a working NLP model in a target language by fine-tuning two relatively small sets of parameters: the core and the specific crammed layer applicable to that language. This approach simplifies large-scale NLP projects and enables seamless language switching by updating a single crammed layer for each language. To validate our proposal, we develop a working NLP model in eight languages and two variants (one general and one tailored to specific domains) and test it on extensive datasets, achieving results that either surpass or match current state-of-the-art performance. Moreover, our research has significant implications for various pressing issues facing multilingual societies, including immigration, tourism, and international trade and communication. Notably, we demonstrate how to create customized NLP models for specific languages or domains with just a few sentences of in-domain text, thereby opening up new possibilities for language adaptation in realistic scenarios. All our codes and models are available online at the following link: https://github.com/yu1011/multi_nlp_with_cvc.

The growing physical separation of communities, as described in "The Big Sort," has contributed to a shift in how people form social connections and gather information. As people have become more isolated from those different than themselves, they have been more likely to engage with sources that mirror their own perspectives and reject those that do not. This phenomenon has created an opportunity for the spread of misinformation among socially isolated groups in search of confirmation, as seen during recent political events. This interplay is the subject of our analysis, which explores the relationship between political misinformation, social isolation, and source confirmation on social media. Our study reveals that individuals prone to spreading false information are often those who are more likely to follow sources that agree with their own views and have limited connections to opposing viewpoints. Furthermore, we identify specific features of Twitter's platform that can contribute to the spread of this type of misinformation, including the tendency to engage more with content that confirms their existing beliefs and retweeting information from trusted sources to their own networks. Our research suggests that the spread of this type of misinformation is a self-sustaining cycle of confirmation bias on social media, fueled by the isolated nature of Twitter's connections, which can result in online phenomena being misunderstood as solely the result of users' individual intentions rather than broader societal dynamics. Our work also reveals that the spread of this type of misinformation is more widespread during major political events, such as elections, and can be further exacerbated by factors like increased online engagement and the popularity of certain Twitter influencers. Our analysis provides a framework for examining the complex factors contributing to the spread of this type of misinformation on social media and identifies areas for future research, including potential strategies for mitigating the consequences of "The Big Sort" on online information dissemination. Our study's results are consistent with the growing body of research that highlights the critical role of social dynamics and platform design in the spread of online misinformation, rather than relying solely on users' individual intentions. Our analysis demonstrates that the spread of this type of misinformation is a collective phenomenon that emerges as a result of simple rules governing users' interactions with each other and the platform, rather than requiring complex cognitive processes on the part of individual users. Our study's methodology is designed to accommodate the ongoing evolution of Twitter's platform and provides a foundation for examining similar phenomena on other social media platforms, such as the spread of information during online protests or the emergence of online memes. To ensure the reliability of conversational systems, thorough testing is crucial. Nonetheless, creating and managing a vast array of tests becomes increasingly difficult as the number of tests grows exponentially with the size of the system, posing a challenge for automated testing frameworks. This paper addresses this issue by introducing a novel approach that compares the conversational experience with a system to the experience with a comparable proxy, either another system or a generated imitation. This method leverages the fundamental concept of equivalence classes in testing theory. By framing the comparison as an equivalence question, it can be answered using a series of yes-or-no questions, significantly reducing the number of distinct tests. This optimization results in a linear increase rather than an exponential one, making it more efficient for large-scale systems. Additionally, this approach yields a tangible benefit for the scalability of automated testing frameworks for conversational systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this innovation through an actual implementation and experimental data showing a marked enhancement in test suite size and overall efficiency. Moreover, our evaluation highlights the value of a system comparable to the one being tested, showing that a system comparable can be either a proxy system or a generated imitation, offering valuable insights for future development in the domain of conversational systems testing. Our research includes an actual implementation of our approach, known as TestDuet, which is an automated testing framework for the API used in dialog management. TestDuet exhibits the advantages of our method through the execution of tests on a real-world application, a virtual assistant named Einstein, alongside a comprehensive evaluation of its own efficiency. Ultimately, our work on this topic is relevant to the broader field of automated testing for systems that interact with humans, presenting a key issue that needs addressing, given the ever-increasing complexity of these systems. It is worth noting that our research is an instance of a more general concept, which can be applied to various analogous scenarios involving system comparisons and equivalence questions, offering novel insights to the testing theory from an unconventional perspective. Our primary goal in this project is to enhance aspect-level sentiment analysis by focusing on user-specific preference. We create a new intricate multi-task learning framework that integrates aspect preference enhancement and sentiment classification. We introduce the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module, an innovative design that accurately identifies unimportant aspects and prioritizes the development of a general user preference representation by enhancing relevant aspects. We conduct extensive experiments on existing datasets and achieve the best results, surpassing the current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, we conduct a thorough ablation study to demonstrate the superiority of GAPE over other comparable designs. We also gather a large-scale real-world dataset consisting of 20,000 user-specific preference sentences and 10,000 test sentences, on which we conduct a difficult aspect-level sentiment classification task and obtain remarkable results. Notably, our approach outperforms the current top-ranked baseline by a significant margin of 12.0% in F-score when applying it to this large-scale dataset. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/zhuzhenhua/GAPE. We also provide the large-scale dataset at this link: https://github.com/zhuzhenhua/GAPE-Dataset. We hope these resources will facilitate further research on the task of aspect-level sentiment classification and user-specific preference learning. We are confident that our approach can be applied to various real-world applications, such as text-based online shopping recommendations and customer relationship management. We plan to explore additional challenges and possible solutions on the following fronts: incorporating more context information, handling explicit and implicit preferences separately, and developing more efficient GAPE-based models. We believe that our approach can be integrated with existing reinforcement learning-based approaches to learn user-specific preferences through continuous interaction, thereby providing more personalized recommendations. We also propose a novel recommendation system based on our approach, which we call GAPE-Rec, and provide a detailed design for the model, the dataset, the evaluation metrics, and the future work, although we recognize that more research is needed on this topic. We aim to investigate the following research questions: how to integrate external knowledge, how to distinguish between explicit and implicit preferences, how to incorporate more context information, how to develop efficient GAPE-based models, how to integrate GAPE with reinforcement learning, and how to evaluate the effectiveness of the recommended items. We propose a novel approach that learns user-specific preferences from text-based feedback, combine the strengths of both hard and soft approaches to learning, provide the code and a large-scale dataset for aspect-level sentiment

Many NP-hard problems have formulations that utilize exotic cones such as polar, dual, or rank-cone constructions in their models. These constructions can be viewed as variations of the original formulation's dimensionality and complexity. This paper explores how the Banach-Alaoglu theorem can be applied to the natural formulations that incorporate exotic cones. By transforming these formulations, we derive equivalent extended formulations. We examine several concrete examples of natural formulations extensively used in practice, and we determine their corresponding equivalent extended formulations. In particular, we investigate how these formulations' dimensions relate to known upper bounds derived from other sources. In some cases, we find that the proposed extended formulations' dimensions are more concise than previously reported records. We anticipate that this paper will add to the current discussion on formulating the Banach-Alaoglu theorem in terms of dimensionality and complexity. It also aims to contribute to the ongoing study of natural and extended formulations in the context of integer programming. We close this comment by noting that the term "exotic cones" refers to a broad category of constructions, and there are many specific variants, such as the polar cone, dual cone, or rank cone, among others. We hope this paper will serve as a starting point for examining these constructions in relation to formulating the Banach-Alaoglu theorem. We also invite researchers to explore and develop new formulations for various problems that can provide additional benchmarks for testing and developing special-purpose integer programming solvers, particularly for testing and developing models that incorporate the Banach-Alaoglu theorem. We believe that the Banach-Alaoglu theorem itself can be viewed as a type of convex set construction, along with the set of convex constructions that can be realized via integer programming. We propose calling the class of constructions that realize the Banach-Alaoglu theorem "BA-constructions" in honor of the mathematicians Stefan Banach and Leonid Vitalievich Alaoglu. We also suggest examining the relationship between BA-constructions and other types of constructions, such as the Hahn-Banach theorem, as well as exploring the connection between the Banach-Alaoglu theorem and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions. We propose investigating the dimensionality and complexity of BA-constructions in the context of specific examples and constructions, with the aim of developing a theory that describes the relationship between the Banach-Alaoglu theorem and the underlying mathematical structures that give rise to BA-constructions. A critical challenge in developing MRI analysis tools lies in creating models that effectively handle new, unseen data. This study investigates how a large, publicly available MRI dataset from healthy subjects can be utilized to develop a model capable of accurately identifying specific brain structures across varying MRI protocols. We evaluated our approach on 3T and 7T MRI scans of the brain, focusing on the caudate nucleus. To make the model applicable across different MRI scanners, we trained it on 3T MRI data, comprising 289 subjects from publicly available sources. This led to a mean absolute error of 0.88 cm^3 when predicting the caudate nucleus volume from 3T MRI scans, and on a separate test set of 100 3T MRI scans, we found a mean absolute error of 1.12 cm^3 when using this model to analyze the midbrain structure. Furthermore, our model demonstrated comparable performance when trained on a substantially smaller private dataset of 20 subjects, indicating its potential as a versatile tool for MRI analysis. This paper introduces a novel network-based framework for solving cooperative optimization problems involving multiple agents. The framework assumes that the value function for the underlying problem can be represented as a convex function with respect to a given set of variables, and that the functional gradients of this representation are computable for any point in the variable space. The framework enables the computation of optimal solutions for various cooperative optimization problems at individual agents without requiring them to cooperate, and it does so in a way that the computed solutions converge to the optimal solution for the underlying problem in a stochastic process driven by its own past computations. The study demonstrates the applicability and efficiency of this framework to a wide range of specific optimization problems, and it provides the underlying conditions under which the associated algorithms guarantee the convergence to the optimal solution for each problem. Furthermore, the study includes numerical results to illustrate the performance of the proposed algorithms, and it reveals that they are capable of achieving the same level of performance as cooperative optimization algorithms while being significantly more flexible and easier to implement. This research was initially presented at the 2022 Conference on Decision and Control. We introduce a robust, efficient model called Motivation Dynamics to enable agents in network environments to achieve cooperation and collaboration. Initially developed for binary decisions, Motivation Dynamics is now expanded to accommodate multiple choices. This multi-agent version demonstrates impressive capabilities in facilitating rendezvous behavior in complex networks. Our results show that, under optimal conditions, Motivation Dynamics can succeed in approximately half the number of steps required for other optimization methods, despite being a relatively simple algorithm. Our research also reveals that Motivation Dynamics can adapt to changing network environments in just a few steps. To further illustrate its effectiveness, we present two application scenarios: coordinating agents in a linear structure and collaborating agents in a circular structure. These examples showcase Motivation Dynamics' ability to efficiently manage large-scale cooperation and collaboration. Notably, our model receives a compelling interpretation in the context of persuasion through mobile agents in sensor networks, making it a practical solution for real-world problems. Our work on Motivation Dynamics also involves exploring the conditions under which the algorithm succeeds or fails, as well as identifying the relationship between its performance and the characteristics of the network in which it operates. Our contributions to this field are reflected in our work being selected as the best paper in the category of algorithms at the 21st ACM Symposium on Parallelism in Algorithms and Architectures (SPAA '19). Our research on Motivation Dynamics has been thoroughly tested and validated, as evidenced by the accompanying experimental code and a simulation toolkit called MD-Sim Toolkit, which is publicly available for the community. This toolkit enables researchers and practitioners to easily replicate our results, extend our work, and apply Motivation Dynamics to diverse real-world applications involving mobile agents. Our aim in sharing this toolkit is to foster further research and development in the field of mobile agent algorithms, as well as provide a practical solution for the specific problem of persuasive advertising in sensor networks known as GreenStream. Our research focuses on the crystal structure and magnetic properties of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds, with an examination of the 4f and 5f element alloy. GdCmSn$_3$ is known to possess a TiNiSn-type structure and exhibit ferromagnetic behavior, whereas CmSn$_3$ is thought to be an antiferromagnetic compound with unknown crystal structure. To study the effects of alloying, we analyzed X-ray diffraction data and investigated the spatial distribution of magnetic moments using the generalized gradient approximation+U method. Sustained effort to grow high-purity CmSn$_3$ crystals was necessary, and we found that increasing Cm content leads to a decrease in the lattice parameters, a distortion of the TiNiSn-type structure, and an enhancement of the magnetic moment. Notably, the magnetic moment per atom in GdCmSn$_3$ compounds approaches that of CmSn$_3$, suggesting that Cm contributes significantly to their ferromagnetism. Moreover, we observed a significant increase in the ab initio calculated moment per Cm atom with rising Cm content, and we attribute this to the half-filled 5f orbital configuration of Cm, which exhibits unique bonding characteristics. Moreover, we propose that CmSn$_3$ compounds hold promise as high-temperature ferromagnetic materials, with improved Curie temperatures achievable through atomic disorder and spin-phonon coupling. We also examined the total and partial magnetic moment distributions in GdCmSn$_3$ compounds using the GGA+U method, and we found that Cm atoms yield the largest moment, with significant spin-orbit coupling effects. We have made our calculation code publicly available on GitHub, along with the X-ray diffraction data. Our study highlights the unique 4f and 5f element alloying effects that give rise to exceptional ferromagnetic properties in GdCmSn$_3$ compounds. We have also explored the potential applications of these compounds in high-temperature ferromagnetic devices, with CmSn$_3$ being a promising material for spintronic technology. We have titled our study "Unveiling 4f and 5f Element Alloying Effects in Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ Compounds through X-ray Diffraction, Ab initio Calculations, and Experimental Evidence" and we have published it in the journal Physical Review Materials. Researchers have utilized the H1 dataset to examine the production of charm and beauty quarks in collisions between electrons and protons at a 31.15 TeV. Both the exclusive and partial production processes of charm and beauty quarks have been studied for the first time in this context, specifically their formation into mesons such as D* mesons, D mesons, and $\Lambda_b^0$ barions. The study found that at higher energies, charm and beauty quarks are produced in greater quantities and that they are likely formed in a short time frame due to the strong interaction force known as the color glue. Additionally, the study confirmed the presence of beauty quarks in proton collisions for the first time and provided initial statistical data on this phenomenon. The research also enabled physicists to test the fundamental principles of quantum chromodynamics in high-energy collisions between fundamental particles. The most comprehensive study of this type to date, it lays the groundwork for future experiments at the Large Hadron Collider that are capable of detecting even rarer beauty quark particles. The study covered 375 picobarns of collision data, which is the largest dataset of its kind to date. The findings also highlighted any discrepancies from predicted theoretical models and may influence the development of future QCD research at the Large Hadron Collider. The study focused on the following reactions: electron-proton collisions that result in the production of D* mesons, electron-proton collisions that result in the production of D mesons, and electron-proton collisions that result in the production of $\Lambda_b^0$ barions. The research established a lower bound for the production process of beauty quarks in proton collisions and provided initial statistical data on this phenomenon. The study compared its findings to existing research on the subject, specifically the TOP Quark Test Beam and the D0 experiment at the Tevatron particle accelerator, which detected beauty quarks in collisions between protons and antiprotons at a 1.96 TeV. The study found that at higher energies, charm quarks are produced in greater quantities than beauty quarks, which is consistent with the predictions of quantum chromodynamics. The study estimated the average energy required to form a charm quark in a proton collision to be approximately 2.24 GeV and the average energy required to form a beauty quark in a proton collision to be approximately 28 GeV. The study also found that a significant proportion of charm quarks are formed in collisions between the fundamental particles that make up protons, known as parton-parton

We derive the exchange laws for the generalized standard Coxeter groups Bn via the approach of translating from the exchange laws of the finite classical Coxeter group Bn to the generalized standard Coxeter group Bn. We then apply this to determine the Coxeter length and descent set of Bn, and show that our results align with existing literature. Additionally, we obtain the exchange laws for the generalized standard Coxeter groups Dn, Fn. We also obtain the Coxeter length and descent set of Dn, Fn, which are yet to be published findings. Based on our analysis, we propose an enhanced approach to defining the Coxeter length, and show that this results in a more streamlined proof when comparing the Coxeter length and descent set of Bn. We also provide an interpretation of the exchange laws for the generalized standard Coxeter groups in terms of root systems, along with an examination of the properties of root systems. We then further investigate the exchange laws for the generalized standard Coxeter groups, which arise from root systems, and determine their Coxeter length and descent set. We also establish that our findings can be applied to a broader class of groups, which we term Lusztig's generalized standard Coxeter groups, and provide an illustration of this concept using the braid groups. We conclude by examining the relationship between the exchange laws for the generalized standard Coxeter groups and the Coxeter length and descent set of the symmetric groups Sn. We also explore the connection between the exchange laws for the generalized standard Coxeter groups and the Coxeter length and descent set of the hyperoctahedral groups Gn. We further investigate the properties of the Coxeter length, and also consider its application to the groups of Lie type, which we term Classical Coxeter groups of Lie type, and discuss some examples, including the example of the Coxeter group E8. We also explore the extension of our analysis to the groups of Lie type, which we term Artin's generalized Coxeter groups of Lie type, and provide some examples, but note that our analysis is not sufficient to determine the Coxeter length of the groups of Lie type, which we term Simple Coxeter groups of Lie type. We conclude our examination of the Coxeter length and descent set of the classical Coxeter groups Bn, Dn, Fn by comparing the results obtained from its definition, its relation to the Coxeter length of the Weyl group W(Bn), and from its exchange laws. A particular optical center known as the T centre has been extensively studied in diamond due in large part to its impressive quantum properties and capabilities. Despite its potential, the T centre has a notable drawback: its emission spectrum can vary significantly, which could make it more challenging to utilize in quantum technology applications. This study investigates the causes of this spectral diffusion, focusing on how it's affected by nearby nitrogen defects and the amount of time the excited state spends emitting, and aims to establish a criteria for creating T centre ensembles with consistent and distinctive optical properties. Such ensembles would be highly desirable for quantum memory devices or other quantum technology platforms. This research paves the way for developing high-quality T centre ensembles held within diamond nanocrystals, which could serve as the fundamental building blocks for several quantum technology applications. This study demonstrates that T centre ensembles located near the surface of diamond can exhibit a unique level of isolation from nearby defects, which could significantly enhance their quantum properties and capabilities. This discovery opens up an exciting possibility of creating a high level of defect isolation by confining T centre ensembles within diamond nanocrystals, which could be an essential breakthrough for several quantum technology platforms, including quantum memory devices. For our object detection model, we suggest utilizing a versatile, context-adaptive object detection framework that can be applied across various domains, including autonomous driving and aviation. This domain-agnostic framework incorporates a hierarchical feature extraction method that divides high-level scene information from low-level vehicle or airbound object details. Additionally, we introduce a novel, self-balancing reweighing technique called Spatial Reciprocal Reweighing (SRR) to address class imbalance issues often found in object detection datasets. SRR's capability to adjust class weights based on the inverse of the number of samples per class, combined with its resistance to overfitting due to the minimal additional parameter requirements, enables our model to effectively manage class weights without relying on pseudo-labelling or similar expensive solutions. Our model's performance is demonstrated through rigorous testing on renowned datasets Francesca and Terra, where it achieves superior results compared to the current industry standards. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/leiwang1988/Context-Aware-Object-Detection. Furthermore, we introduce a newly created, publicly accessible terrestrial object detection dataset called Terra, comprising 10,000 manually annotated images. Terra has a diverse range of settings, including roads, airbases, brownfields, and remote nature reserves. Its data split consists of 7000 training images, 2000 validation images, and 1000 evaluation images. It's worth noting that our code framework is also applicable to the detection of airbound objects, and we recommend checking the accompanying paper for more details. With the Terra dataset, we have made significant improvements to the current industry standards, as validated by extensive testing. This new dataset, along with the validated code framework, are both accessible online at the aforementioned GitHub link. We also invite researchers to collaborate with us in addressing various challenges associated with large-scale object detection databases. We have made our Terra dataset publicly available for download at the following link: https://github.com/leiwang1988/Terra-Dataset. We are committed to continuously upgrading our object detection model in response to evolving challenges and new research findings. We look forward to collaborating with the research community on this engaging topic. This paper investigates solutions to the elliptic system of partial differential equations: $u_v = f_1(v,u)$, $v_t = f_2(u,v)$, where the functions $f_1$ and $f_2$ are continuous and satisfy certain growth conditions. When the domain is bounded and the functions $u$ and $v$ belong to a specific continuous function space, we prove the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the system. Furthermore, when the domain is unbounded and has a finite measure, we establish the existence of a unique solution to the system. Additionally, we investigate the case where the domain is unbounded and show that the system can be transformed into a singular elliptic system defined on the bounded domain $\Omega \cup \{0\}$, for which we establish local existence, uniqueness, and regularity of solutions. This generalizes previous results by enabling the value $0$ to be any real number. This extends previous work by Li and Niu, who dealt with the specific case where $f_1(v,u) = u_v$ and $f_2(u,v) = v_t$. This also builds upon the results by Díaz, Gállego, and Vailent, who investigated a system with the form $u_v = f(v,u)$ and $v_t = f(u,v)$, but with a greater function growth condition. This growth condition allows for a more general application of the Schauder estimate in obtaining local $C^2$-regularity of solutions to linearized systems. This estimate is achieved through an extension of the regularity result by Guelpen and Vailent and the use of the Holder continuity of the function $f$, for which we introduce a new proof to accommodate a more general case than that presented in Guelpen and Vailent. This new proof relies on the use of the Holder continuity of $f$ to obtain the Schauder estimate. This extends the previous work of Guelpen and Vailent, who dealt with the specific case where the function $f$ is constant. This also generalizes the result by Cabre and Sire, who investigated a singular elliptic system defined on the bounded domain $\Omega \cup \{0\}$ with the value $0$ being $1$. We establish new concentration inequalities for independent Bernoulli random variables, considering their sum as a given parameter. These results apply to both convex functions of these variables and polynomial expressions in them. The achievements can be applied to provide improved concentration bounds for specific scenarios involving independent Bernoulli random variables. As an example, we derive improved tail estimates for the number of successes in a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials, each with a specified probability of success. Furthermore, we obtain generalized results that yield concentration inequalities for the number of successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, each with a varying probability of success, conditioned on the total number of trials, which is shown to be suboptimal by a factor of approximately $\log n$ compared to the best known bounds. These findings are then used to obtain enhanced concentration inequalities for the maximum of a set of independent Bernoulli random variables with a common range of values. We also touch on the related topic of concentration inequalities for combinatorial structures encoded by random graphs, specifically focusing on the study of the concentration of the number of edges in random graphs at a given average degree. We demonstrate that both standard superconcentration with a weak tail estimate and an improved result with stronger tail control can be obtained as special cases of our general result, which involves a specific random graph process known as the random graph process known as the binomial random graph $G(n,p)$, albeit with some minor restrictions. In all the above-mentioned instances, our primary tool is an innovative application of the large deviation principle for empirical measures of random samples, combined with the properties of convex functions and polynomial expressions. Our achievements also build on the notable works by Cramér, Cherno-Var, and Talagrand, which are utilized as critical components of our proof methods. We believe our independent Bernoulli random variable results can be viewed as an expansion of the concentrated bounds obtained by Cramér, as well as the results related to combinatorial structures that arise from random graphs, which are analogous to the specialized findings for specific distributions obtained by Borell, Cramér-Rüdiger-Rao, and Scheideler. Our general approach can be seen as an extension of the concentrated bound approach for specific distributions, which typically involve the application of the Cramér-Cherno large deviation theory in combination with the properties of convex functions and polynomial expressions. We have thoroughly examined the method for classifying the equivalence classes of non-degenerate symplectic similitudes under the symplectic group Sp$_2n(Q)$. This analysis involves establishing a comprehensive framework of invariants, which are then used in a three-part process to categorize the equivalence classes. Initially, we distinguish between two distinct types of forms: one is a non-degenerate symplectic form, while the other can be either a positive-definite quadratic form or a negative-definite quadratic form. Secondly, we determine the determined the number of times the non-degenerate symplectic form must be scaled in order to obtain the set of invariants that classify the equivalence classes. Lastly, we establish the relationship between the scalar factor and the two types of forms. This relationship is represented as the product of two factors: the first corresponds to the set of invariants, while the second set corresponds to the equivalence classes of positive-definite quadratic forms in an (2n+1)-dimensional vector space over Q. This enables us to connect our classification system to the existing framework of lattices of positive-definite quadratic forms, which are denoted as $\Lambda^{+}_{2n+1}(Q)$. Consequently, we can rephrase the problem of classifying the equivalence classes of non-degenerate symplectic similitudes as determining the elements of $\Lambda^{+}_{2n+1}(Q)$ that identify the set of invariants for a given non-degenerate symplectic similitude. This leads to a natural extension of the concept of lattices to non-degenerate symplectic similitudes, which we have denoted as $\Lambda^{S}_{2n+1}(Q)$. This represents the set of tuples consisting of a non-degenerate symplectic form and a set of invariants defined on the integers plus one. Our analysis addresses the complex problem of organ acceptance decisions in kidney transplantation, which we approach through the lens of value function in a Markov Decision Process. By treating incompatibility as a dynamic state variable, we provide a simplified framework that enables us to incorporate various factors, including donor characteristics, compatibility issues, and waiting time. Within this model, we seek to maximize the expected utility of receiving a suitable kidney, taking into account the outcomes of sending, accepting, or rejecting an offered kidney. By examining the optimal policy for a general case, we derive conditions under which it is always optimal to accept compatible offers immediately. Furthermore, we establish bounds on the value function, which facilitate its approximation through linear interpolation. These advances enable us to develop an efficient algorithm based on linear value function approximation, which outperforms existing policies in extensive simulation tests involving real-world data. Our research demonstrates the significance of considering incompatibility as a state variable and presents tangible guidelines for policymakers and healthcare professionals managing kidney transplantation networks. It also highlights the potential applications of reinforcement learning in solving related organ allocation problems. Ultimately, our work paves the way for further enhancements, such as incorporating additional factors like organ quality and specialized matching algorithms. It is noteworthy that our model assumes an infinite supply of donors, whose waiting time is essentially zero, in order to focus on the core issues of organ matching and incompatibility. However, future work will be necessary to extend and refine this model to address these limitations and other organ transfer scenarios. Our algorithm execution was conducted on the Desktop Cluster Computing Platform maintained by the Knowledge and Knowledge Institute at the University of Waterloo. This study examines how word embeddings, specifically using the Word2Vec model, misclassify certain financial terms, particularly antonyms like "bull" and "bear," as similar or equivalent. Our analysis reveals that these embeddings learn frequentist patterns instead of probabilistic relationships and tend to prioritize trendy terms over crucial vocabulary, leading to subpar performance in tasks like sentiment analysis. We propose a novel approach, named the Hyperbolic Sentiment Network (HSN), utilizing hyperbolic space to represent antonyms as distinct nodes connected by an edge, and shows significant improvements in processing financial texts, particularly in resolving the antonym issue, and demonstrates comparable results to the BERT model when applied to general text data. Our results highlight the benefits of HSN in addressing the antonym classification challenges faced by traditional embeddings and highlight the potential advantages of hyperbolic space in modeling semantic relationships within financial texts. We also explore alternative applications of HSN to a variety of problems, including multi-class classification, graph-based classification, and graph-based collaborative filtering, and find that it can effectively tackle difficult classification problems involving complex relationships between categories. We make our code and models publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/happyhac/HSN. Our results also demonstrate the efficacy of low-dimensional hyperbolic embeddings in reducing the dimensionality of feature spaces while preserving crucial information, and we make our code and models publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/happyhac/HSN. We introduce the concept of eliminative learning, where agents selectively shun actions that are deemed unessential by observing others' behavior in variable decision-making situations. This approach is shown to lead to the elimination of iteratively dominated actions, even when confronted with complex, dynamic environments. To achieve this, we developed ELM, a trailblazing algorithm that enables agents to identify and disregard superfluous actions by utilizing the observed frequency of others' actions, combined with a novel utilization of the relative entropy. Through theoretical and empirical analysis, ELM is demonstrated to successfully navigate diverse challenges, including those involving uncertain outcomes, multiple agents, and hidden action structures, all while successfully excluding dominated actions from their repertoire. Furthermore, ELM's performance is compared to other renowned algorithms in various scenarios, showcasing its superior problem-solving capabilities. The underlying mechanism of ELM is also explored to provide valuable insights into the design of future learning algorithms capable of handling complex, dynamic environments efficiently. These environments often feature action dominance relationships that can shift over time. To support the implementation of ELM, a complementary toolkit is made available, enabling users to configure customizable learning environments according to their specific requirements. These environments can be both simulated and managed using real-world data. To further illustrate the applicability of ELM in real-world settings, a case study is conducted using a financial dataset, and the results reveal that ELM is capable of uncovering the optimal investment strategies in dynamic market conditions. These conditions are characterized by constant change, making it difficult for other algorithms to adapt effectively. In contrast, ELM is shown to be highly adaptable, capable of learning from experience and Consequental Knowledge, making it an attractive choice for various real-world applications. This paper presents a new ensemble method known as Ensemble DGLAP, which is effective in constraining the properties of parton distribution functions (PDFs) when fitting data across various energy scales. PDFs evolve over energy scales through the DGLAP equation, and our proposed ensemble method accounts for this evolution by dividing the DGLAP evolution matrix among the PDFs in our base PDF ensemble. Our approach allows for a more efficient exploration of the parameter space and prevents extrapolation outside the physical range of PDFs during the fitting process. Furthermore, we observed that the method enables a direct comparison of PDF properties at different energy scales and facilitates the inclusion of PDF constraints from other experiments with different energy ranges. Our study demonstrates that Ensemble DGLAP yields comparable or better fit results compared to traditional methods for various scenarios, including lattice PDF determination, global PDF fitting, and PDF fitting from a single deep-inelastic scattering experiment. Our implementation of the Ensemble DGLAP method is publicly available within the PDFfitting framework called PDFfittingBase, which can be downloaded from GitHub. We also released our final Ensemble DGLAP-generated PDFs set, known as A18-EDGLAP, on the PDFMC website. This new ensemble method is valuable for contemporary PDF fitting tasks and is anticipated to be beneficial for future PDF fitting endeavors. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, all relevant codes and inputs used in this analysis have been thoroughly documented and made publicly available on GitHub and the PDFMC website. This enables users to access the methods and inputs used in this study and to utilize the developed code in their own PDF fitting projects. This code package can be found at the following web address: https://github.com/PDFresearch/PDFfittingBase. We introduce the variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework, a general method that reformulates policy gradient estimation problems. This formulation leads to the derivation of methods that reduce variance when sampling from stored experiences. The resulting algorithm, specifically tailored to utilize the developed variance reduction techniques, is shown to converge to the correct policy gradient. Theoretical support for our proposed VRER framework is provided by analyzing the convergence of an illustrative algorithm. Furthermore, we develop a straightforward policy gradient algorithm utilizing importance sampling, which is then applied to a representative experience replay setting. The resulting solution is proven to be statistically consistent and efficient in practice. The proposed solutions are evaluated using extensive numerical experiments. The code used in these experiments is available openly and allows for easy customization. We have developed a novel algorithm called MG-GLAM for constructing gravitational look-up tables on meshes, specifically tailored for N-body simulations with gravitational interactions. This method leverages fundamental properties of gravity, particularly the falling ray technique, in conjunction with advanced geometric library tools, to achieve significant performance enhancements. Compared to the established Multigrid Gravity algorithm, MG-GLAM exhibits improved speed and accuracy with the same precision settings, thus enabling faster N-body simulations. Furthermore, MG-GLAM demonstrates superior stability and versatility, enabling the integration of various external forces and customized gravity behaviors with mesh-based methods, whereas earlier codes were less adaptable in this regard. This work is accompanied by open-source code and concrete benchmark results to guide further improvements in this area. Overall, MG-GLAM represents a computationally efficient and highly adaptable solution for modeling complex gravitational interactions in various simulation contexts. This code has been utilized to evaluate the performance on high-performance computing systems and microbenchmarking, in addition to extensive real-world applications. This research is applicable to various domains, including astrophysics, fluid dynamics, and biology, as well as other fields with similar N-body simulation requirements.
