We introduce the chordal SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$ process in mathematical analysis, which is a variant of the Chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) defined for $\kappa\geq0$ and an additional parameter $\rho\geq0$ within the unit circle. This new model involves a random curve that originates from the union of two horocyclic disks and fills a region in the complex plane as time progresses. We demonstrate that this new model is a Markov process, which enables us to determine its ultimate outcome as time approaches infinity. This leads to a classification of the chordal SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$ process into three distinct categories based on the values of $\kappa$ and $\rho$. This result is accompanied by geometric insights into the targeted surface in the complex plane, which we refer to as the target surface. This surface maintains distinct properties for specific values of $\kappa$ and $\rho$, including being a disk, a parabolic domain, or a Schlicht region that contains a disk. This result is further expanded to a larger set of applications in mathematical analysis, leading to new insights into the targeted surface. This result is also applicable to a broader context of the dynamic flow of horocyclic disks within the complex plane. This result is derived through the analysis of the radial part of the chordal SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$ process, which is interconnected with the dynamic flow of horocyclic disks. This allows us to extend our findings to this broader context of the dynamic flow of horocyclic disks. This extension is a valuable contribution of our study. articles. By integrating features from issue trackers and version control

projects involving multiple contributors, but it is beneficial for any

develop and refine the TextMapDrive algorithm for human navigation, which

can be applied to any wiki-based website. The code for WorkingWiki is

To analyze complex interactions in turbulent reacting flows, researchers often rely on simplified combustion models. Within the linearized framework, one such model has been found to perform effectively and stems from a double-explosive reaction scheme. This particular model was derived using a novel method that involves manipulating the reaction scheme's kinetics to achieve desired properties, thereby meeting application requirements. In the context of linearized combustion theory, this model exhibits unique features that set it apart from other models, including constant heat release rates across all reaction rates. To demonstrate its practical utility, this model was applied to a canonical, chemically sensitive, and globally unstable scenario, resulting in a perfect match between linear predictions and actual data. Furthermore, by employing this model, significant improvements were achieved in accurately simulating certain characteristics of this scenario, specifically the location of the neutral stability curve. This was accomplished by employing a high-resolution numerical method that was capable of accurately resolving the small-scale fluctuations present in this scenario. Overall, this model has been found to offer a superior alternative to traditional single-step combustion models and provides a more realistic representation of constant heat release rates, thereby offering valuable insights into the dynamics of unstable waves and their interactions with turbulent flows. Consequently, it is anticipated that this model will assume a key role in the analysis of various application scenarios. To obtain this model, a reaction scheme with two consecutive reactions was employed, along with a closure law that relies on the reaction rate being equal to a constant value of one. This approach ensures that the model reacts as if there are two explosions occurring within the reaction time scale, thereby justifying the designation as a double-explosive reaction scheme. It is worth noting that this model does not actually utilize a two-step reaction scheme to deliver its results, but rather a single-step scheme with a specific kinetic model that mimics the properties of a two-step reaction. This model has been found to be highly effective and can be used within a linearized framework, but it is not suitable for use within nonlinear applications. It is also noteworthy that this model does not include any sort of thermal feedback, but rather constant heat release rates across all reaction rates, and as such it has been designated as a reference model for comparison with other models. It is anticipated that this model will be employed as a standard reference model for the purposes of assessing the stability of chemically sensitive waves in turbulent flows. We investigate the implications of ultralight dark matter connected to neutrinos and examine its effects on the cosmos during the early stages. As this dark matter interacts with neutrinos, it influences their behavior, particularly in the post-big bang era. We analyze multiple scenarios of its coupling to neutrinos, considering both their individual and collective interactions. In the process, we delve into how this coupling affects the neutrino dark matter component, which may take the form of either a stable oscillon-based component or one that eventually disappears due to the neutrinos' rapid thermalization. We also explore the potential for this dark matter to leave identifiable signatures in the cosmic microwave background and its variability. Moreover, we investigate how this scenario might influence standard model particles and other dark matter components, which could, in turn, impact the formation of the large-scale structure of the Universe. We conclude by discussing the avenues for further research in this field. This study paves the way for examining the effects of this scenario on both massive and massless neutrinos within the context of their own self-consistent equations. This leads to a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of this dark matter model in the early Universe. This analysis also highlights the limitations of the simple harmonic oscillation approximation commonly employed in the study of ultralight dark matter. This study further reveals the conditions under which the coupling of neutrinos to this dark matter component results in their temporary decoupling from the rest of the Universe, which in turn could explain specific observational features of the cosmic microwave background. This study also illustrates the potential for this scenario to give rise to unique signatures in the cosmic microwave background, which could potentially be confirmed by upscaling the current large-scale structure simulations to incorporate both massive and massless neutrinos within this specific dark matter model. This study finally highlights the potential implications of this dark matter model for the formation of the large-scale structure of the Universe. This study also shows that the effects of this dark matter model on both massive and massless neutrinos can be examined by solving a system of two self-consistent equations, which in turn require a combination of an initial conditions provider and an root finder. This study utilizes the envelope method to generate the initial conditions for these equations, which in turn were solved using the Newton-Raphson method. This study also employs the leapfrog algorithm to solve these equations, which in turn were validated against the results obtained using the Newton-Raphson method. To gain a better understanding of how genetic variations affecting specific traits influence proteins, we examined the impact of protein sequences on phenotype-associated SNPs across 29 different traits using a comprehensive dataset. Our investigation uncovered significant correlations between the frequency of phenotype-associated SNPs influenced by protein sequences and various traits, with particular emphasis on traits influenced by both protein sequence and SNPs within coding regions. Furthermore, we identified distinct patterns of protein sequence influence on phenotype-associated SNPs for each trait, demonstrating the utility of our approach in unraveling complex genetic interactions. Our findings also revealed substantial traits whose phenotypically associated SNPs are primarily influenced by non-coding regions, suggesting that such traits harbor key insights for resolving the "genetics-environment" paradox. Our research provides a foundation for exploring the underlying biological mechanisms of these traits and related conditions, as well as other comorbidities that may share similar genetic interactions. Ultimately, our results demonstrate the value of our method for uncovering specific genetic interactions associated with each trait and condition, and showcase the potential for this approach to contribute to a deeper comprehension of human genetics. Our dataset and analytical framework are now publicly available, enabling the comprehensive reanalysis of our findings and facilitating exploration of this approach for uncovering genetic interactions associated with other conditions or traits of interest. To that end, we have made our code and dataset available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ourresearch/psns. Our research discovered a significant increase in strange particles, particularly $K^*$ and $\Lambda^*$, produced in proton-proton collisions at the LHC.  These findings support our theoretical model, which explains the phenomenon of quark gluon plasma decomposition based on temperature-dependent parton thermalization and collective flow.  We contrast our results to two prominent theoretical approaches, the Thermal Yang-Mills theory and the Star/PHENIX collaboration's results from nuclear collisions.  Furthermore, our findings predict enhanced production of exotic charmed strange particles, such as $D^0_K^*$ and $\Lambda_c^+$, in future charmed hadron experiments.  These predictions are expected to be confirmed by existing and future LHCb and ALICE experiments, which are equipped to detect rare charmed hadrons produced in proton-proton and heavy ion collisions. Consequently, we anticipate the production of exotic charmed strange hadrons, which involve rare $c s$ quark combinations, will exhibit the same thermal characteristics, thereby validly using our calculated collective hadron ratios to predict the discovery channels of $D^0_K^*$ and $\Lambda_c^+$.  Notably, the production of these exotic charmed strange hadrons is expected to be primarily discovered through the $D^0_K^*$ meson, given the larger production ratio of $D^0$ over $\Lambda_c^+$ particles, which is attributed to the limited acceptance of the ALICE detector in heavy ion collisions, and the presence of background events in proton-proton collisions. A similar argument can be applied to these binaries based on their radio emission properties. Since about half of NMXRBs are thought to be radio pulsars, we estimate the population of radio pulsars in the Galactic bulge to be around 2500 to 2800. This prediction was subsequently confirmed by search surveys of radio pulsars in the Galactic bulge, revealing a population of approximately 2400 millisecond pulsars within the same region. This convergence of results and data sets provides the most convincing evidence yet for the bulge's pulsar population being primarily composed of low-mass X-ray binary pulsars that have spun up through accretion of a companion star. Quantum mechanics governs the behavior of matter at its most fundamental level, and its precise control can lead to the development of novel chemical reactions and materials. However, controlling individual quantum states in complex molecules remains challenging due in large part to the fast dephasing of quantum coherence caused by vibrational mode coupling. Researchers have discovered that specific vibrational modes linked to quantum states might hold the key to enhanced chemical reaction control and have identified key pathways for optimizing these modes to slow the dephasing of quantum coherence. By leveraging these findings, a general theoretical model has been developed to calculate the dephasing rates of quantum states in molecules with coupled vibrational modes, and it has been applied to a study of cyanoethynelithium - a highly reactive and short-lived compound. Computational simulations demonstrate a 104-fold decrease in dephasing rate calculations when employing appropriate vibrational mode coupling optimization techniques, and this approach can be used to investigate a broad range of molecules and chemical reactions. Furthermore, researchers have proposed an optically pumped quantum drive that can manipulate quantum coherence and thereby control chemical reaction barriers, and it has been applied to an examination of the cyanoethynelithium ethylene chem reaction, an reaction with high reactivity and fidelity requirements. Consequently, this study opens up an interdisciplinary path that fuses theoretical chemical physics, chemical knowledge, and quantum drive engineering for the design of optimized molecular quantum drives capable of controlling complex chemical reactions efficiently. This approach might also provide a framework for developing new chemical reactions with novel products and higher yields, as well as contributing to a better comprehension of the interplay between quantum mechanics, chemical reactivity, and environmental influence. This research has been published in the journal Nature Chemistry and is part of an ongoing effort to develop a molecular quantum drive that can control ethylene cycloaddition reactions. This effort is a part of a larger program aimed at exploring the boundaries of chemical reactivity and developing new catalytic mechanisms for the safe production of C--C coupled molecules. Human dialogue involves more than just exchanging facts; it also requires exploring various dialogue topics and adjusting the flow to suit changing circumstances. To mimic this diversity in automated dialogue systems, we introduce a new metric called Doc Diversity, measuring the set of relevant documents as a proxy for the range of topics to be explored in the conversation. We then develop a novel generative adversarial network (GAN) to enhance document diversity in generated responses. Our diversity-enhanced GAN incorporates multiple artificial separators in the discriminator's structure to identify distinct sub-documents and associated ad-relevance labels. As a result, this model outperforms the baseline in various assessments of response quality and diversity. To further improve performance, we propose a simple yet effective data expansion technique called Lexical Expansion (LE), involving the synthesis of artificial training data with preserved document structures and label variations. Evaluations across multiple settings confirm the effectiveness of our diversity-enhanced GAN and the LE technique. We have made the code and models publicly available to facilitate future research in this area. To gauge the practical applicability of our diversity metric and methods, we conduct thorough human evaluation tests, with a large portion of the results presented in this research remaining unpublished to date. To ensure transparency, we have included the detailed evaluation protocol in the supplementary materials. To promote further development in this area, we have released our diverse GAN models and related code at https://github.com/ASCLaboratory/Diversity_GAN. To facilitate additional human evaluation tests, we have created a web-based evaluation platform at http://diversity-evaluation.com/. To access the pre-processed dataset used in our experiments, please visit the WebNLG 2017 repository at https://github.com/agenteam/webnlgEvaluationData. To access the Lexical Expansion technique used in our experiments, please visit the WordSenseInduction repository at https://github.com/ASCLaboratory/WordSenseInduction. To note, the term "document" is used interchangeably with "sentence" in this research, given the nature of the WebNLG dataset employed. We have made the following supplementary materials available: the code used in the GAN development, the LE technique, and the web-based evaluation platform. We have also made the following data sets available: the WebNLG 2017 dataset, the Lexical Expansion technique data set, and the generated data sets utilized in the human evaluation tests. We have made the following results available as supplementary materials: the results presented in the human evaluation tests conducted across multiple settings.

We have thoroughly examined the influence of angular momentum on hydrogen burning in low-mass objects, encompassing brown dwarfs, neutron stars, and brown star scenarios. Our study utilized a comprehensive model that accounts for the objects' internal temperature distributions and varied their angular momentum through changes in initial spin velocity. To validate our approach, we compared our results with existing research on the angular momentum upper limit for hydrogen burning in neutron stars. Our findings reveal a distinct "kink" in the relationship between angular momentum and cooling age, coupled with a critical angular momentum milestone beyond which objects begin to lose hydrogen through the Rayleigh-Taylor instability. This research also explores the distinct settings under which objects transition from hydrogen retention to hydrogen depletion, leading to either cooling curves with kinks or those with spin-down accelerations. Furthermore, we outline possible detection methods for such objects through increased $^{7}Li$ abundance in neutron star crust, as well as hydrogen depleted, cool white dwarf remnants. Ultimately, our analysis highlights the diverse outcomes for low-mass objects depending on their initial angular momentum, mass, and composition, paving the way for observational verification of these predicted phenomena.

A bipartite graph can be modified to create a planar double crossover (PDC) by dividing specific vertices and connecting them in a particular way. This process ensures that the resulting PDC maintains the original edge weights. A key aspect of this method involves identifying the minimum number of vertices to split, which we'll refer to as the splitting number. We establish an upper bound for the splitting number, showing it is always less than the minimum number of vertices needed to represent the graph in a linear order, combined with the cyclomatic number of the graph. This achievement is made more significant by the fact that this upper limit can be achieved through a specific algorithmic process. A key component of this research also explores the relationship between the splitting number and other key parameters of the bipartite graph, including its cyclomatic number, maximum degree, and minimum degree. We demonstrate that the smallest possible value for the splitting number can be obtained by removing loops and by splitting specific vertices of highest degree. This enables us to generalize this approach for other types of graphs that are variants of bipartite graphs. This variant graph includes double crossover trees, planar reticulata, and grid graphs among others. We establish lower and upper bounds for the splitting number of each of these graph types, which are more specific cases of bipartite graphs. This research provides a foundation for further exploration of the splitting number in more general contexts. We also introduce a new concept known as double crossover trees, which offers an innovative application of the splitting process for bipartite graphs. This new concept has the distinction of being the most basic form of a planar double crossover, making it a significant discovery in the realm of graph theory. We believe that the methodology developed in this research will find utility in the fabrication of specific types of DNA structures known as double crossovers, particularly within the confines of a three-dimensional space. This can be achieved by first representing a set of four points as a map, followed by an investigation of the conditions under which double crossovers can form between specific pairs of points, which are defined as the points for which the distances between each other and the two remaining points are equal. This problem has implications for the study of four-point DNA chemistry, which is an area that is yet to be fully understood. This study examines how bipedal robots utilize feedback from their surroundings to adapt to uneven terrain as they navigate through gait cycles. To simulate the physical interactions between a bipedal robot and its environment, we use a Morton model to create a variety of terrain types with diverse textures and heights. By incorporating the displacement of the foot into the robot's control system, we enable the robot to modify its movement in response to the intense forces experienced during ground contact. As the robot moves, its feet interact with the Morton model terrain, affecting the distribution of pressure and the formation of holes on the surface. Our analysis reveals that the robot's ability to adjust its movement over time is significantly affected by feedback from the ground, resulting in varying degrees of efficiency, diversity, and robustness in different scenarios. Additionally, we find that the robot often creates unique patterns of pressure and hole formation on the surface with distinct structures, and these structures can be either random, regular, or a combination of both. Our observations also show that the robot's movement is capable of inducing changes in the surrounding environment that influence its future movement, an phenomenon we describe as "memory" in the system. Ultimately, our study highlights the interconnectedness of the robot's movement and the environment, demonstrating that the relationship between them is more complex and interconnected than previously understood. Our results are also relevant to other dynamic systems that exhibit self-sustaining movement and feedback interactions with their surroundings. Our research was conducted using a combination of computational simulations and physical experiments with a robotic walker navigating through various terrain scenarios. Our findings have implications for developing control systems that enhance the resilience of bipedal robots in dynamic environments. Our approach to modeling the robot's interaction with the environment is also applicable to the study of other complex feedback systems. Our research shows that feedback from the environment is crucial for achieving efficient movement patterns in bipedal robots, and that these movements can create unique patterns of pressure and hole formation on the surfaces they interact with. Our study explores the interconnectedness of the robot's movement and the environment with the help of metrics that quantify the diversity, robustness, and variability of the feedback loops within the system. Our approach to studying the interconnection of the robot and its environment as a complex system of feedback loops is similar to the approach used in the study of another system of feedback loops, the Amazon rainforest, in the book "The Language of the Grandes Floods" by Philippe Clain. We analyze the logical properties of the power series field $k[[x^{-1}]]$ in an infinite field $k$. Since an infinite field satisfies any polynomial equation, we must consider fields with a specific characteristic. If the characteristic is positive, we investigate this property in the context of a total residue map and its connection to first-order logic. If the characteristic is 0, we show that a related statement is undecidable, even when restricted to a specific subclass of fields, unlike the case of characteristic p > 0 where we can determine decidability based on field properties. Given its undecidability in characteristic 0, we examine a related problem that is equivalent to a well-known problem but in a different mathematical context. This context allows us to draw a contrast with the case of characteristic 0. Additionally, we establish some connections between this contrast and the differences in the computational properties of two related formal languages, which were previously unknown to the best of our current knowledge. Furthermore, we outline the steps to extend our analysis to a broader class of fields known as Hensel fields. These fields include the power series field $k[[x^{-1}]]$ and other fields of formal powerseries in non-identically zero variables, within any characteristic. We also establish the connection between the logical properties of these fields and the decidability of two related formal languages, which were previously undecidable in the 1970s. We have successfully increased the limitations of our current knowledge in this area by an order of two and have made significant progress towards increasing these limitations by an order of ten. We have made this progress by using new approaches that are different from the standard mathematical techniques used in the related field of algebraic geometry. We have used these new approaches to discover some previously unknown contrasts between two subfields of algebraic geometry that were previously thought to be similar. We have also used these new approaches to establish some connections between the power series field $k[[x^{-1}]]$ and another field known as the field of Puiseux series. We have used these connections to re-examine some of the results established in the 1960s by algebraic geometers working in the subfield of positive characteristic. Last year, researchers introduced HyperFetch, a technique that enables side-channel
extraction from main memory at a secondly level precision for the first time, using
only a single trace. This led to an accessible Flush+Reload attack for the first time.
However, creating a more effective attack through HyperFetch's current form proved
impossible. This paper leverages Cloud Providers' memory management features to
develop HyperDegrade, an improved version of the previous attack. By modifying
memory settings, HyperDegrade enables more precise side-channel extraction on a
kernel-level, allowing for attacks on memory protected by Flush+Reload methods.
Consequently, HyperDegrade is capable of carrying out a successful Flush+Reload
attack on a single attempt for the first time, reducing the number of required
traces from an unlimited amount to just one trace. Additionally, this solution
enables attacks on high-security targets that were previously inaccessible.
Furthermore, HyperDegrade enhances time precision to a secondly level for the first
time, making it feasible to launch an attack on a specific time frame with high
accuracy. This outcome is achieved by exchanging massive amounts of memory with
limited data, making the attack more discreet and harder to detect. This research
also uncovers various cloud providers' memory behavior and reveals how different
memory settings affect side-channel leakage. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how
easy it is to launch an attack on an unsecured environment and the challenges
of launching an attack on a more secure environment. This discovery motivates
cloud providers to review their memory management security policies. This research
was conducted using real-world cloud infrastructure and resulted in actionable
advice for both cloud providers and security-conscious applications. This advice
includes how to configure memory settings to minimize side-channel leakage and
how to develop secure applications that can withstand side-channel attacks in cloud
environments. This research was performed with the assistance of cloud providers
and involves actionable guidance for the community at large. This finding is
particularly significant for security-conscious applications and cloud providers,

The notion of twist doubles is applied to various knotted structures including virtual knots, linkings in virtual space, and braid knots. This paper demonstrates how to modify twist doubles through a process called diagonal moves, which allows for the transformation of specified knotted structures into others. It is observed that the set of diagonal moves forms a group, enabling the incorporation of additional known knotted structures into the category of twist doubles. Furthermore, it is shown that the braid representation of a knotted structure can be made more simplistic through the application of diagonal moves, resulting in a variety of twisted doubles. The paper also explores relationships between twist doubles and other knotted structures, including Turaev's construction of virtual knots and the formation of braid knots from linkings in virtual space. Additionally, necessary and sufficient conditions for a knotted structure to be a twist double are established, along with a virtual knot that satisfies the required conditions but cannot be represented as a linking in virtual space. The paper concludes by discussing the relationship between volume doubles and twist doubles. The volume double of a knotted structure refers to the linking in virtual space obtained through the application of a specific process called volume crossing change. It is proven that the volume double of a knotted structure is a twist double, and vice versa. The paper also explores additional properties and representations of volume doubles. The development of the volume double construction also led to the discovery of new properties of volume crossing change. A particular class of integrated cocycles from quantum group coefficients yields quantum invariants for knots. The study examines how combining these cocycles through conjugation relates to their invariants and shows that this process is linked to the integrality of the quantum Casimir element in quantum groups. The research also explores how this connection behaves under different integration methods for cocycles. The primary focus is on the quantum cocycles arising from the Drinfeld-Jimbo U_q(g) and its relation to the quantum invariants, specifically the Jones polynomial. The study reveals that the standard U_q(g) cocycles do not define distinct quantum invariants for knots when integrated, as they behave in the same manner as the 2-cocycle coming from the quantum central functionals. The result can be generalized to other quantum groups of the Dynkin classification, but does not extend to the braid group cocycles. The study concludes by exploring the implications of these findings for quantum invariants and the quantum Yang-Baxter equation. The main results are further illustrated through examples of U_q(g) for n=2,3. The associated Java applets can be found at the study's website. We investigate the dynamics of a multi-agent system consisting of agents that can switch between two roles, providing services or requesting them within a role-switching framework. The performance of the system is assessed based on the time agents spend on tasks of varying levels of difficulty. To understand how the distribution of task difficulties influences the adoption of role-switching strategies, we use the evolutionary game theory approach. The resulting model exhibits multiple equilibria, showing that the optimal strategy depends on the specific characteristics of the system. We also analyze how changes in the variables affecting the payoffs obtained from providing or requesting services impact the adoption of corresponding role-switching strategies. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications of this model in contexts such as crowd sourcing and mobile ad-hoc networks. To better understand the dynamics of the model, we conduct numerical experiments that provide valuable insights into the conditions necessary for the coexistence of all possible role-switching equilibria. These experiments also reveal the existence of a stable state characterized by an unusually long duration of role-switching, which we term the ``role-switching plateau''. To explore the properties of this plateau state, we conduct additional numerical experiments that involve manipulating specific variables of the model. These experiments reveal the existence of distinct plateau states corresponding to different difficulty levels of tasks, as well as the existence of a threshold beyond which the system enters the plateau state. We also investigate how changes in certain variables of the model affect the onset time of the plateau state, as well as its duration. Finally, we discuss the policy implications of our findings for practitioners seeking to manage crowdsourcing platforms and mobile ad-hoc networks. The appendix contains an in-depth analysis of the spatial version of the model. The simulation code used to obtain the experimental results is available online at https://github.com/yilu-li/rgtss. The code was written using the SciPy library version 1.10.1 and the NumPy library version 1.20.2 for the numerical experiments, and the NumPy library version 1.20.2 for the data analysis. This paper delves into the privacy risks associated with vertical federated learning, where multiple organizations collaborate to build a comprehensive machine learning model while keeping sensitive information confidential within each organization. Theoretical attack strategies targeting specific protocol variants were developed to illustrate privacy vulnerabilities in vertical federated learning. These attacks successfully breached the privacy guarantees of several widely-used protocols, including blinding-based and cryptonic methods. Furthermore, the study proposes an enhanced protocol that incorporates cryptographic techniques to prevent precise attribute-based attacks, thereby enhancing the privacy of vertical federated learning. Experimental results showed that this protocol can efficiently prevent privacy breaches and provide a high degree of privacy protection, even when faced with large-scale datasets. The proposed protocol was also found to be computationally efficient and scalable for massive data sets, making it suitable for widespread practical applications. This includes a comprehensive case study examining its feasibility in a real-world scenario. The study's findings were further validated by a privacy assessment leveraging the MIPI privacy metric, which revealed a substantial improvement in privacy protection when compared to the standard protocol. This was demonstrated by a notable decrease in the attacker's success rate when attempting to guess sensitive information about the data set. This achievement was made possible by incorporating additional cryptographic operations that counteract the increased computational overhead, allowing for accurate attribute prediction to be prevented in vertical federated learning settings. This allows researchers to build trust in machine learning models without compromising security and privacy, as demonstrated by a representative example showing that a model built using the proposed protocol correctly classified 99% of new instances while ensuring the confidentiality of sensitive information. This makes the protocol suitable for widespread practical use, including a real-world scenario examined in the study. This scenario involves building a machine learning model to predict the health conditions of cows based on a large dataset shared by multiple cattle farmers, a scenario that is representative of vertical federated learning settings in the agriculture industry. This represents a representative application of the proposed protocol but does not limit its applicability to other domains such as finance and healthcare. We examine the connections between Pseudo Random Fourier Features and traditional kernel methods, specifically focusing on the example of the Gaussian kernel. Our analysis reveals that PRFFs are analogous to selecting specific grid points to approximate a function, which is similar to choosing specific feature dimensions from the original set. We further demonstrate that many common kernel methods can be viewed as employing specific subsets of Fourier features. Our results also demonstrate that PRFFs are superior to RFFs in both reduced dimensionality and improved predictive performance. We further investigate the relationship between the PRFFs and the underlying data, discovering that the optimal solution is linked to the location of the mean vector in the feature space. Our analysis also reveals the limitations of using PRFFs with positive semi-definite kernels, such as the Gaussian kernel, due to the introduction of noise in the feature space. We provide examples of kernels that are free from this limitation, including the linear kernel and the polynomial kernel. Our experiments with real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of PRFFs over RFFs and traditional kernel methods. We also introduce an iterative method for determining the optimal set of Fourier features, which further enhances the performance of the PRFFs. Our approach is made available as an open-source tool on GitHub. Our results also demonstrate the applicability of the approach to large-scale datasets by analyzing the feature dimensions required for a range of datasets from the NIPS Feature Selection Challenge. Our method is capable of handling datasets with up to 500,000 instances, which is a significant improvement over the current iterative method with a maximum of 20,000 instances. This research paper examines the circumstances under which a specific type of higher-dimensional hypersurfaces can maintain a constant scalar curvature when transformed through a conformal change. Within the context of an $n$-dimensional hypersurface residing within an $n+2$-dimensional space, we investigate how a particular M\"obius transformation affects its scalar curvature and derive an inequality that defines a broad class of such transformations. By utilizing our previous findings on the conformal invariance of certain higher-dimensional surfaces, we extend existing records to derive the solution to an Euler-Lagrange equation related to the scalar curvature, thereby determining its minimum possible value. As a result, we obtain a lower bound for the minimum scalar curvature that a compact, conformally flat hypersurface can maintain with any given size and dimension. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this minimum scalar curvature can be achieved by specific types of compact, conformally flat hypersurfaces, thereby classifying them as the sole family of hypersurfaces with constant scalar curvature across all dimensions. This research also provides an alternative proof for the optimal embedding of certain types of compact, conformally flat hypersurfaces in higher-dimensional space. In the process, we rectify an error in the current record for the upper limit of the difference between the square of the maximum curvature and the minimum curvature of compact, conformally flat hypersurfaces with any given size and dimension. This new limit is more stringent and is determined by a constant that is directly proportional to the minimum scalar curvature of these hypersurfaces. This finding further highlights the significance of our previous research on the lower bound for the minimum scalar curvature of these hypersurfaces. Our analysis focused on a random process where the removal of a single node leads to a chain reaction known as an "avalanche." To gauge the impact of these avalanches, we tracked how the resulting changes fragment the network into isolated components. Our findings revealed that the size of avalanches influences the rate at which the network components merge, with increased post-incident connectivity observed during large avalanches. Conversely, a node removal in a network prone to extensive fluctuations often triggers avalanches that significantly increase the distance between the remaining network components, leading to prolonged recovery times. Additionally, our research demonstrated that the relationship between the average distance between network components and the size of avalanches exhibits a power law. Ultimately, our study highlights the crucial impact of post-incident network dynamics on recovery outcomes in temporal networks. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the conditions leading to the formation of highly disconnected networks are similar to those resulting in the phenomenon of "snowballing" often observed in temporal networks. We introduce the concept of a sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, an innovative variant of the Michelson-Sagnac interferometer designed to enhance sensitivity in measurements of gravitational waves. By modifying the traditional Sagnac interferometer to incorporate a liquid-filled cavity within its test mass, the new design manages to surpass the Michelson-type interferometer's sensitivity in the low-frequency domain, while matching the Sagnac interferometer's performance in higher frequency ranges. This innovative configuration translates to a frequency-dependent threshold between 10^-3 Hz and 10 Hz, below which the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer outperforms all other laser interferometer standards, making it an appealing option for ground-based gravitational wave detectors operating at low frequencies. Additionally, the sloshing-Sagnac design exhibits improved sensitivity in high-frequency settings, making it a viable alternative to the standard Sagnac design for space-based gravitational wave measurements. Notably, the development of a sloshing-Sagnac interferometer also paves the way for creating a low-frequency Michelson-Sagnac design, which could potentially serve as a bridge between Michelson-type and Sagnac-type interferometers. This research was physically realized and verified through successful testing of a prototype at the 40m Mark II test bed in Hanford, Washington. The resulting data showed that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's sensitivity matches theoretical predictions, demonstrating the practical feasibility of this innovative concept. The work described herein is relevant to ongoing and future laser interferometer standards, including the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, and provides a foundation for the development of even more advanced variants of the sloshing-Sagnac design. The associated data and analysis code are accessible through the Gravitational Wave Open Software Facility. The physical test bed used in this research is also available for scientific collaboration at the 40m Mark II test bed in Hanford, Washington. A novel copper compound called GaCu3(OH)6Cl2 has been synthesized and studied, demonstrating unconventional magnetic behavior. Contrary to the prevailing theory, this material's magnetic interaction appears to be antiferromagnetic in nature, arising from direct interactions between the spins of individual copper atoms. To understand this phenomenon, a comprehensive theoretical analysis was performed, showing that GaCu3(OH)6Cl2's unique crystal structure allows for unusual spin interactions that prevail over competing ferromagnetic interactions between neighboring spins. This discovery has been validated through the use of advanced theoretical models, which reveal that this material occupies a rare and distinct region of the phase diagram, characterized by the coexistence of Dirac electrons and strong correlations between its spins. These features make GaCu3(OH)6Cl2 particularly interesting for the study of complex many-body phenomena and its potential to give rise to novel phases of matter. Despite being an antiferromagnet, this compound exhibits unusual spin dynamics, suggesting that its spin interactions may not be static and that its behavior could be more complex than initially anticipated. To fully understand its physics, further research is necessary, but it has the potential to give us a deeper insight into the relationship between spin, electron behavior, and material composition. This finding could also pave the way for the development of novel materials that exhibit unconventional physics and may have potential applications in the field of quantum electronics. This discovery was made possible through the use of advanced X-ray scattering techniques that allowed for the detailed analysis of this material's crystal and magnetic structure at the atomic level. This knowledge was then used in conjunction with theoretical models to simulate the behavior of this material's spins and electrons, and to identify the unique features of its composition that give rise to its distinctive properties. This comprehensive understanding was achieved through the collaborative efforts of an international research team consisting of scientists from the United States, Europe, and Asia, who utilized a range of techniques including the growth of single crystals, X-ray scattering, thermal expansion, heat capacity, magnetic susceptibility, NMR, and theoretical modeling to analyze this material. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has searched for evidence of heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) in final states with two osmic charged leptons and a missing energy component. To achieve this, five HNL production scenarios were examined, and the limits set on the masses of these particles were found to be as high as 875 GeV for the case of through-production of tau HNLs. Furthermore, future experiments at the High-Luminosity LHC and the 100 TeV Future Circular Collider are projected to lower the effective lifetime limits to $10^{-13}$ seconds, thereby increasing the detection limits for heavy neutral leptons with masses up to 1.5 TeV and 3.5 TeV for the Standard Model case, and to $10^{-12}$ seconds for low-mass HNLs produced via leptoquark decay. This study highlights the significance of considering HNLs that decay into muons and tauons in future experiments, as the existing optimized search strategies primarily focus on the production of electron HNLs in the muon and tau channels. Additionally, the analysis demonstrates that the effective lifetime limits can be effectively lowered by searching for HNLs in the decay channel involving two tauons, particularly in the case of through-production of tau HNLs. To this end, a comprehensive reconstruction of the tautau channel was implemented for the first time in the ATLAS experiment, utilizing advanced techniques such as deep neural networks, and the results showed that this channel is highly promising for discovering HNLs with masses up to 600 GeV and effective lifetimes of $10^{-12}$ seconds. Our studies used a vast machine translation corpus and a sophisticated generative model, and the results showed that NRM performed significantly better in both source-to-target and target-to-source language generation tasks in comparison to baseline methods. Furthermore, NRM was found to be highly effective across diverse translation directions and large text summarization data. Our proposed method ourperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques including Neural Machine Translation, Enhanced Neural Attention, and Knowledge Distillation, while maintaining an efficient training scheme by simply starting from the pre-trained $n$-gram models, thus making it highly suitable for vast datasets. 3D face reconstruction is a highly challenging task in computer vision, especially when attempting to construct an accurate 3D face model from a single image, considering the limitless possible orientations an image can take. Previous studies have achieved notable success in this area by utilizing deep learning models, yet these methods generally lack the capability to decompose a 3D face into two distinct components: those that remain consistent across different head orientations and those that change as the orientation varies. In response to these limitations, this paper introduces a novel framework titled Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), capable of regressing a set of orientation-dependent and orientation-independent factors from a single, freely-oriented 2D face image. These factors, regressed in a self-aligned manner, enable the reconstruction of a 3D face model from any orientation, thus offering a more direct and aligned approach as opposed to the conventional method of utilizing pose estimation techniques. Experimental evaluations conducted on extensive 3D face datasets demonstrate that the proposed method delivers superior results in comparison to existing techniques for 3D face reconstruction and facial structure analysis. Additionally, the proposed model is shown to be effective in a real-world application setting, characterized by limited training data and explicit pose constraints, as validated through results obtained on the VGGFace2 dataset with a focus on reconstructing high-resolution 3D faces in the wild. In this setting, the model is trained with data constrained to a specific orientation, yet it surprisingly exhibits the ability to accurately generalize to unconstrained orientations, thus proving the efficacy of the proposed approach. Implementation details, qualitative and quantitative results, as well as thorough ablation analyses are thoroughly discussed in the paper. In conclusion, this research proposes a pioneering technique for 3D face reconstruction from a single oriented 2D face image, presents an exhaustive experimental evaluation of this approach, and provides an explicit code base for further research in this area. This code base is publicly accessible at this link https://github.com/zhai-lab/SADRNet. This paper presents a novel spell correction approach that leverages a crude dictionary, and we demonstrate the significance of this method in a specific application. Incorrect spellings in hand-filled election forms can significantly impede optical character recognition, thereby hindering efficient tabulation. To mitigate this issue, we developed a spell correction algorithm for this domain, and in testing, it showed a 10-point NIST score improvement over the base line optical character recognition performance. We also analyzed the algorithm's performance with different preprocessing methods for the input text, and these experiments guided the creation of a dictionary utilized in the spell correction algorithm. This dictionary, in turn, was used to correct the most prevalent spellings in election forms, which in turn led to a 20-point NIST score improvement over the base line optical character recognition performance. We open-source this spell correction algorithm to aid other applications with accuracy demands similar to election tabulation. These applications often involve a limited scope or specific vocabulary, which facilitates the creation of an effective dictionary for spell correction. We also provide a comprehensive evaluation of the algorithm's effectiveness in various settings to ensure its suitability for similar use cases. This algorithm can be categorized as a non-recurrent neural network-based spell correction algorithm due to its reliance on a fixed dictionary in spell correction decisions. We term it a crude dictionary spell correction algorithm, and it is distinct from other Recurrent Neural Network-based algorithms in the same domain. This algorithm is particularly useful in domains with limited vocabulary and data, and it has the added benefit of providing intuitive insights into the underlying mechanics of spell correction. These insights are valuable for the fine-tuning of the algorithm and the evaluation of its performance. To facilitate widespread adoption, we also open-source a voter tabulation spell correction dataset that we created specifically for this algorithm, and it comprises 12,500 words extracted from 5,000 hand-filled election forms in the United States. These words are characterized by incorrect spellings that can impede optical character recognition, and they originate from various election jurisdictions across the country. We also provide a corresponding set of corrections for each word to serve as a golden standard for the evaluation of the algorithm. These words and their corresponding corrections can be integrated into the training and testing datasets for the algorithm, and they are specifically designed to reflect the vocabulary typical of election forms in the United States. We believe that this dataset will be valuable not only for the voter tabulation application but also for other spell correction algorithms in a similar context. We also explore the integration of the algorithm with a base line optical character recognition

As the frequency of extreme weather events increases, storing energy becomes a vital adaptive strategy for mitigating renewable power fluctuations and maintaining grid stability. In response to this need, we developed a new model that depicts risk-aware energy storage as a dynamic process, taking into account the unpredictable effects of severe weather conditions. In testing this model, we discovered that high levels of risk aversion could lead to storage devices that, instead of adapting to changing weather conditions, remain idle in response to extreme temperatures, resulting in substantial societal costs due to increased CO2 emissions. Based on this finding, our research suggests that policymakers should prioritize managing storage devices in a way that reduces their risk aversion, thus enabling these devices to effectively adapt to the ever-changing weather conditions and resulting in greater societal benefits. Furthermore, our study reveals that by implementing policies that reduce storage devices' risk aversion, it is possible to decrease CO2 emissions from the energy sector by up to 10% and 20% in cold and warm climate extremes, respectively. Additionally, we found that such policies could be highly effective, with the payback period for storage devices ranging from 2 to 5 years, thus presenting an attractive option for future policy-making efforts. In evaluating our results, we considered various scenarios, including different storage costs, CO2 pricing, and weather patterns in multiple regions worldwide. Ultimately, our research underscores the critical role that risk-aware energy storage can play in the energy sector and highlights the potential societal benefits of policies designed to manage storage devices' risk aversion. To facilitate this research, we developed a new mathematical model that incorporates adaptive behavior from storage devices and assessed the societal implications of this behavior for future low-carbon energy systems. This model has been made publicly available online. This research builds upon our earlier study published in the journal Nature Climate Change, but it differs from that study by primarily focusing on the evaluation of policy interventions aimed at managing risk-aware energy storage rather than examining the impacts of extreme weather conditions on such storage. This study extends the methodology used in the earlier study by employing a mix of data sources, including the Solar Radiation Streamer, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, the National Renewable Energy Laboratory's System Advisory Model, the Carbon Pricing Dashboard, and the Global Energy Transition Outlook. Precise control over the quantum states of two-qubit systems is crucial for implementing various logic operations in quantum computing.  Two-qubit gates like the controlled-NOT (C-NOT) and the controlled-phase (C-PHASE) gates are fundamental components that require the state manipulation of two qubits.  This study investigates the performance of two-qubit C-NOT and C-PHASE gates made from silicon double quantum dots.  By calculating the gate fidelities using a full stochastic simulation, we analyzed the effects of qubit connection methods, donor placement, and tunnel coupling on our results.  Our findings show that a C-NOT gate can be realized with a high success rate of over 98%, while a C-PHASE gate with high fidelity requires tighter constraints on donor placement.  Additionally, our study identifies the optimal placement of donor atoms and the corresponding charge states of the quantum dots to achieve the desired outcomes for both gates.  Ultimately, our research provides a practical framework for executing two-qubit logic operations with silicon double quantum dots, offering a realistic pathway towards large-scale quantum computing with silicon devices. Deep learning models for natural language processing have shown significant potential when incorporating additional, artificially created data. Various techniques such as phrase replacement, sentence removal, and word substitution are already effective for this purpose, but more research is necessary to explore other methods that guarantee similar performance gains. An investigation was conducted to analyze three untested data augmentation strategies – combining cross-lingual dictionaries, utilizing a generative adversarial network, and generating language pairs based on bilingual lexicons – for their effectiveness in enhancing the performance of deep learning models. Contrary to expected results, neither of these methods demonstrated enhanced model performance when applying standard technique parameters, indicating a higher likelihood of these methods being beneficial when employing optimized technique parameters. Consequently, the development of more advanced data augmentation techniques will depend on a thorough, parameter-specific optimization of each method. Furthermore, this investigation uncovered an unexpected aspect of the GAN-based method, revealing it to be a type of denoising autoencoder, thereby providing valuable insights into NLP tasks using GANs. Additionally, an important consideration in utilizing GANs for data augmentation was identified – the necessity to utilize training data sets that are highly homogeneous with respect to the target task. If not, GAN-based data augmentation may lead to a decrease in model performance. Notably, an evaluation of the Consistency Loss technique from the field of few-shot learning was not performed, as it is a more general approach that provides consistency among samples generated by the same class label, thereby offering no distinct advantage over standard training on NLP tasks. This research is significant because it represents the first comprehensive investigation of unconventional data augmentation strategies for the enhancement of deep learning models in NLP tasks, and it reveals the possibility that many other untested methods are available for this purpose. In this research, three specific methods were analyzed in depth. Nevertheless, a broader perspective is advocated, suggesting that the evaluation of any untested data augmentation technique must be conducted with caution, considering various factors such as the underlying algorithm, the characteristics of the model being evaluated, and the specifics of the target task. Moreover, it was observed that many untested methods are likely available, implying that research in this area remains unfinished and in need of further exploration. In this context, the 36-fb inverse data set from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV is analyzed to investigate the characteristics of top quarks. The investigation focuses on measurable quantities such as the top quark transverse momentum, the charge of the W boson decay products, and the MET (missing transverse energy). This paper delves into the analysis of privacy breaches in a type of machine learning known as differential private learning, specifically focusing on graph-structured data. To gauge the severity of a privacy transgression, we examine the maximum possible privacy loss, which can be a difficult problem to solve due to the intricate connections between data points in graph structures. We simplify this challenge by converting the problem into a maximization problem that can be solved using a cut-based linear programming technique, though we acknowledge that this approach may not always yield the most intricate pathways of graph structures. Nevertheless, we provide a subsequent algorithm that refines our earlier analysis to obtain a more precise solution by exploring these complex graph relationships. This research is applicable to various applications involving graphs, including protein interaction networks and social media connectivity maps. We demonstrate the practical utility of our method by applying it to an actual problem involving a cardiovascular disease risk assessment model based on electrocardiogram data. Notably, our approach can be used in conjunction with other differential private learning methods, including the exponential mechanism and the GP-IP method. We also highlight the theoretical guarantees of our method, which provide an upper bound on the maximum possible privacy loss in a way that is both general and applicable to various specific settings. We make our code publicly available to facilitate the reproducibility of our results. We anticipate that our research will contribute to the development of a new class of cutting-plane linear programming techniques that can be employed to compute the maximum possible privacy loss in a broad range of scenarios beyond the specific case studied here. We also propose a novel algorithm that enhances our initial analysis and retrieves the maximum graph cut, which we term the BCDCut algorithm. We anticipate that the BCDCut algorithm will find utility in various applications, including but not limited to, the identification of complex graph structures, as well as the analysis of multi-cut problems in general. In this work, we investigate a specific knowledge distillation method that employs a Teacher-Student architecture, where a lightweight student network learns from a more advanced teacher network, with the goal of surpassing the performance of a high-capability teacher network in a multi-classification-task setting. Due to the inherent difficulty in training, knowledge distillation often requires the teacher network to be well-trained beforehand. We contend that this assumption is no longer necessary when employing Teacher-Student architecture and aim to prove that the student network can effectively teach the teacher network the essential knowledge, thereby improving the teacher network's performance. To validate our hypothesis, we employ a Teacher-Student architecture in a knowledge distillation framework and employ the student network to teach the teacher network on two classification tasks that are combined into a single task. Our results indicate that this method enables the teacher network to achieve a performance boost on the combined task with only a 2-layer network as the teacher network and achieves state-of-the-art performance when the teacher network has more layers. Additionally, our method demonstrates flexibility when combined with other knowledge distillation techniques and allows for the incorporation of additional information to enhance the learning process. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/TS_KD.

Bucket Elimination is an esteemed inference algorithm in graphical models, notably efficient when dealing with large datasets. However, the standard Bucket Elimination approach requires the ability to optimize subproblems quickly, which can be challenging in certain situations. To address this difficulty, we introduce a new algorithm called Distributed Bucket Elimination, tailored for processing large data sets across multiple servers. Each server executes a modified Bucket Elimination variant, with the ability to solve smaller subproblems locally. The algorithm dynamically manages the breakdown of subproblems among servers and retrieves the necessary messages to solve the overall problem. We establish the convergence of our algorithm and provide an accompanying theorem, along with an analytical estimate of the number of iterations required. Furthermore, we derive non-trivial guarantees on the size of the subproblems and message costs, enabling our algorithm to leverage existing efficiency bounds of Bucket Elimination in specific settings. Experimental results demonstrate our algorithm's capability to efficiently handle large-scale probabilistic models by scaling in terms of the size of the data. Our code is openly accessible online.

This issue has significant implications for public sector professionals working in policy-making, urban planning, social services, and community development, among others. These professionals must be aware of the possible presence of algorithmic bias in Web search results and consider alternative information sources, such as academic databases, to ensure they access the most accurate and reliable information possible for their work. A proposed rCASPR sampling method reduces the number of measurements required for phase contrast imaging while minimizing the point-spread function and associated image contrast losses. The technique leverages a sparse representation framework and a combination of cascade algorithms to generate a compressed set of data that can be used to produce high-quality phase contrast images. In comparison to traditional linear sampling, rCASPR yields a 10 times decrease in point-spread function and a 100 times decrease in measured count rates. This method demonstrates particular advantage in rCT applications where low-energy X-rays predominate and phase contrast imaging is particularly valuable for enhancing contrast in low-density materials. In a simulated CT scan of a 10 cm thick water sample using 50 keV X-rays, rCASPR was found to provide comparable image contrast to that obtained with phase contrast CT using 20 times more measurements and demonstrate notable point-spread function improvements over traditional sampling methods. In addition to CT scans, rCASPR can be applied to other phase contrast imaging techniques such as radiography and tomography using focused beams. We have developed a precise statistical testing method known as the paired-permutation test, which allows us to accurately determine whether the ordering of two sets of data is significantly different. This test involves all possible permutations of the combined dataset, making it computationally intensive. Alternatively, we can employ a Monte Carlo approximation to achieve a faster computation time. However, the Monte Carlo method may not provide accurate results in certain situations. The new paired-permutation test has been implemented exactly or approximately in various existing algorithms. In this paper, we present an algorithm for executing the paired-permutation test exactly, which is highly efficient and able to outperform the Monte Carlo approximation in various applications. This new algorithm was created to support the evaluation of molecular signatures in relation to cancer patient survival rates. We used this algorithm to investigate the paired-permutation test on twenty different molecular signatures, which included seven signatures derived from subtypes of glioblastoma, six signatures derived from subtypes of breast cancer, and seven signatures derived from subtypes of colorectal cancer. Notably, this algorithm has broad utility extending beyond the specific context of this research. It is particularly useful in situations where we need to exact testing of a specific permutation hypothesis that involves a substantial portion of the dataset, the entire dataset, or the combination of multiple datasets. In such scenarios, the Monte Carlo approximation is typically unreliable due to the limited number of samples generated, leading to inaccurate test results. We explore a connection between loom spaces and singular simplicial complexes in n-dimensional space. Our findings reveal that a loom space over an open set in n-dimensional space can be broken down into its most basic components - simplexes that combine to form the space's structure. This relationship provides a new way to understand the topological characteristics of loom spaces. Additionally, our research reveals that a particular type of triangulation, which we refer to as a lexicographic triangulation, can be associated with every loom space and reflects its unique topological features. The relationship between loom spaces and singular simplicial complexes in n-dimensional space also provides the basis for further investigation into the subject of singular simplicial complexes. Furthermore, our research on loom spaces and singular simplicial complexes in n-dimensional space can be extended to weigh the importance of specific triangulation types, leading to an examination of the subject in (n+1)-dimensional space. We also establish that any singular simplicial complex in n-dimensional space can be converted into a loom space over an open set in n-dimensional space, thereby establishing an equivalence between the two subjects. We conclude our research by exploring the relationship between singular simplicial complexes and loom spaces in (n+1)-dimensional space, discovering that any singular simplicial complex in n-dimensional space can be transformed into a loom space over an (n+1)-dimensional space, thereby establishing their equivalence. This research was initially presented at the 2011 ICCOER conference held in India. This research employs machine learning techniques on a comprehensive dataset, which includes 42 widely used technical indicators and historical stock price data for a 12-month period, to predict daily stock price fluctuations over a 1-day period for 8 notable companies listed on the S\&P 500 index. A regression-based model was utilized to analyze the relationships between these indicators, past stock prices, and the resulting predictions for stock price movements. The findings indicate a positive correlation between indicators such as Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) and stock price increases, as well as a negative correlation between indicators like Bollinger Bands and price rises. Furthermore, the study reveals that certain indicators like Relative Strength Index (RSI) exhibit non-linear effects on stock price predictions. A comparison of machine learning models revealed that Random Forest yielded the most accurate predictions for stock price fluctuations. This study's results also highlight the limitations of technical indicators in predicting stock price movements with high accuracy, and suggest that other factors such as company performance, management decisions, and market sentiment may influence stock price fluctuations. This research provides a comprehensive baseline for the prediction of daily stock price fluctuations at a company-specific level. The data showed that the object overpowers the gravitational force holding the grains together and escapes the stuck state, experiencing extreme drag due to violent tremors caused by its sudden movement. The distance it travels before the drag returns to a steady state is highly dependent on the speed at which it's moved and how quickly the grains move past each other. This study provides first-time evidence of a similarity in the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow $v_3$ and elliptic flow $v_2$ for different identified particles. To quantify the similarity, we introduced a ratio $R_{32} = \frac{v_3}{v_2 \sin(3\phi_p)}$ based on the event plane's correlation between $v_2$ and $v_3$. We found $R_{32}$ to be essentially independent of transverse momentum and particle type, albeit with some variation due to $p_T$ ranges and the types of particles studied. Furthermore, we observed $R_{32}$ to be comparable across midrapidity for different centrality classes, and it was also found to be comparable at forward rapidity for the most central proton-proton and lead-lead collisions, exhibiting a certain degree of universality. This similarity in $R_{32}$ also extends to the transverse momentum dependence of anti-protons in the most central proton-proton collisions. We interpreted these findings in the context of the interplay between initial state fluctuations and particle scattering dynamics. Estimating optical flow is a fundamental computer vision task that facilitates various applications and advanced vision algorithms. While self-supervised flow estimation methods have achieved notable successes, several challenges remain to be addressed, including the impact of occlusions. In this paper, a novel self-supervised flow estimation framework is introduced that leverages a context encoder to represent complex scene elements, including those hidden by occlusions. The proposed method, called Context-Aware Optical Flow Estimation (CAOFE), utilizes a contrastive learning technique to correlate forward and backward flow fields, enabling the context encoder to capture precise flow information, including for elements behind occlusions. Unlike current self-supervised flow estimation approaches that focus on reconstructing synthetic motion fields, CAOFE generates real-world correspondence maps between frames, producing a more accurate and robust representation of flow information. In addition, CAOFE incorporates an occlusion-aware loss function to minimize the influence of occlusions on flow estimation. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that CAOFE achieves superior flow estimation results on various datasets, particularly in challenging scenarios with significant occlusions, despite the known limitation that current datasets lack adequate occlusion diversity. To rectify this limitation, a new dataset has been created specifically for evaluating flow estimation algorithms in the presence of occlusions, contributing a valuable resource to the computer vision community. This dataset, called the Optical Flow with Occlusions Dataset, comprises extensive real-world occlusions, setting it apart from existing datasets that primarily represent artificial occlusions. Systematic ablation analysis and qualitative evaluation provide valuable insights into CAOFE's performance and potential areas for improvement. With its promising results and the large theoretical gap yet to be bridged in handling real-world occlusions, the proposed method serves as an engaging starting point for further research in this unexplored domain. Intercepting system calls at the kernel level allows operating system techniques like virtualization and sandboxing.  However, implementing system call filtering for applications written in interpreted languages like PHP and Python is complicated.  Most Linux systems employing user-space system call filters use programs written in C or similar languages to intercept system calls.  To address this issue, we created Timeloops, a system call filtering technique for applications running on interpreted languages.  Timeloops rewrites the system library functions that applications use to interact with the operating system.  It achieves this through a novel use of Linux's Library Call Interpositioning feature.  We put Timeloops through trials to evaluate its performance.  It shows that Timeloops provides fast system call filtering with minimal overhead, meeting our system call filtering speed baseline.  As for other interpreted languages, we outline the modifications required to adapt Timeloops for them.  Lastly, we outline the limitations of this technique along with potential security risks.  Our research demonstrates that system call filtering is possible on unmodified applications written in interpreted languages like PHP and Python.  To facilitate this research for others, we made the source code of Timeloops publicly available.  We also contributed the Timeloops code to the community working on Linux system call interception.  Furthermore, we specified and contributed modifications to the Linux kernel that enable Timeloops to function on unmodified Linux distributions. We propose a decentralized method for tracking unknown objects using a team of sensors with limited fields of view, reducing the computational requirements for detecting and predicting the positions of undetected targets. This approach utilizes a dynamic set of filters to account for the limited visibility of each sensor, resulting in a convex optimization problem to solve for predictions. We then establish the convergence of our method, demonstrating that the predicted positions converge to the actual positions of the targets at a rate proportional to their distance from the observing sensors. To evaluate our approach, we develop a decentralized implementation using multiple sensors with limited visibility and test it against existing methods in simulated scenarios with varying complexity. These experiments show that our proposed method tracks targets more accurately than alternative approaches, achieving lower computation costs according to various scaling metrics. Furthermore, we illustrate the applicability of our method to a real-world scenario, showing that it can effectively navigate a radar system with limited fields of view. We also make our code publicly available to facilitate further research.

A major issue with time-domain wavefields in FD full waveform inversion arises from the increasing amplitude as simulation time progresses, causing elastic simulations to diverge quickly and making it challenging to apply. We transform the time-domain problem into the frequency-domain to mitigate this issue by leveraging the constant amplitude property of frequency-domain solutions. This leads to a new frequency-domain formulation for elastic FWI, eliminating the need for time-domain simulations and addressing the problem of growing amplitudes. This new formulation enables the use of existing frequency-domain solvers and elastic impedance inversion algorithms. We also introduce a strategy to connect the frequency-domain formulation to the time-domain framework commonly employed in seismic simulation software. This connection allows incorporating various frequency-domain results back into the time-domain framework for continued simulation and data comparison. We demonstrate the feasibility of this frequency-domain formulation for elastic FWI through numerical examples featuring realistic seismic data sets and realistic models. These examples showcase the applicability of this method for incorporating multiple-frequency-domain solutions into an interpolation framework, as well as the effectiveness of the FWI algorithm applied to a single frequency or frequency interpolation. We also examine the impact of different initial models on the inversion process and present a scenario where the frequency-interpolation method helps to overcome the model's local minimum problem. We conclude that the frequency-domain formulation provides a viable alternative to the time-domain approach for elastic FWI, especially when dealing with complex geological structures requiring multiple simulations to reach convergence. We make our Python code publicly available to facilitate further research in the field of FWI.
