In the process of knowledge amalgamation, a student model is trained to excel at a task by utilizing multiple teacher models that excel at different tasks. If there are many teacher models available, using them all can become inefficient. To address this issue, we developed an approach where we first generate a saliency map for each data point across the tasks, taking into account the relationships between tasks. These saliency maps enable us to prioritize the most relevant data points for the student model and exclude the rest, even if they pertain to unrelated tasks. When the number of tasks is substantial, this method allows us to incorporate a significant amount of knowledge effectively. We tested our method across three scenarios and discovered significant gains when there are many tasks with limited data, and improvements over traditional methods in scenarios with an abundance of data. Notably, our method demonstrates the capability to combine tasks of different sizes with ratios of 1:10 and 1:100, surpassing existing knowledge distillation techniques. We also observed that our approach can be applied to incorporate knowledge from multiple tasks about the same data when there are different expert models available. To validate our method's effectiveness in this scenario, we conducted experiments that showed our approach leading to significant improvements over traditional knowledge distillation techniques. We open-sourced our code and saliency maps generation method to facilitate further research in knowledge amalgamation. To our knowledge, this is the first method that is capable of effectively combining knowledge from multiple tasks with the highest number of tasks tested (100) and multiple models per task (10). Our method's efficacy is demonstrated across six datasets, including three text datasets and three image datasets. Our knowledge amalgamation method's robustness is showcased with novel scenario scenarios that have minimal research available. Our approach builds upon our previous research published in IJCAI 2023. We've derived an irremediable general entropy production equation for quantum systems following quenching incidents. This novel equation connects the change in system entropy to both the initial and final temperatures, as well as the specific heat capacity of the quantum system in question. Furthermore, our investigation uncovered distinct cases where the produced entropy may either reach equilibrium with the surrounding environment or remain distinct, depending on certain conditions. These conditions are determined by the sign of the difference between the heat capacities of the system and its surroundings. We've also established that the minimum irreversible entropy generation occurs when the system's temperature coincides with that of its surroundings. This finding can be viewed as an extension of the Clausius-Peres inequality to its analogue in the quantum domain. Our research on entropy generation was conducted within the framework of quantum thermodynamics. The developed entropy production equation can be applied to diverse quantum systems, including both discrete and continuous systems comprising multiple components. It is especially relevant for detecting phase transitions within these systems following quantum quench events. We also validated our results using both analytical and numerical methods, including NISHE (negative infinite sum to the end) approximation, which is a widely accepted technique used to calculate heat flux within quantum quench scenarios. Some examples of phase transitions detected using our entropy production equation are exhibited in both fig 2 and fig 3 of the accompanying paper. We believe our entropy production equation has the potential for broad applications in quantum quench scenarios involving diverse complex systems following abrupt changes, especially in the context of non-equilibrium phase transitions. The associated JCM heat flux data and numerically simulated SU(1,1) heat flux spectra are also made available for use by the scientific community. The relevant HEURISTICS and NUMERICAL SIMULATION data are listed in tables 1 to 4 of the current paper. These include the works presented in ref [24,25,29,32,35]. We investigate the time-dependent distinguishability of systems undergoing non-unitary dynamics, where the unitary part of the total system includes both the system of interest and its surrounding environment. To compare the evolution of different states within the system's unitary component, we define a distinguishability measure that accounts for the twirling of the initial system-plus-environment state over time. Our analysis focuses on a two-level system within its electromagnetic environment and explores various initial conditions to see how they affect the duration for which differences remain detectable. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of distinct environments on this time frame and find that the distinction can be explained by the curvature of the system's energy spectrum. Additionally, we observe a connection between the time frame during which the system's behavior is indistinguishable and the introduction of spontaneous photon decay. Our research demonstrates that the time frame for which the system's behavior remains distinguishable can extend far beyond the typical 10 million times the Planck constant over the photon energy, when the system's energy spectrum exhibits non-negligible curvature. Our results also highlight the limitations of the typical approximation used to calculate the spontaneous decay rate. Researchers examined the effects of three surface treatments on silicon: etching the surface, combining etching and oxidation of the surface, and oxidizing the surface alone. To analyze these treatments' impact on carrier concentration near the surface, researchers employed SIMS, AES, and four-point probe testing. Compared to etching the surface, carrier concentration was significantly reduced when the surface was oxidized, both near the oxide/silicon interface and within the silicon bulk. This indicates that oxidizing the surface can minimize free carriers and aid in fabricating silicon-based UV detectors. Fitting carrier concentration profiles to the Shockley-Hall model revealed that this model effectively describes distribution of free carriers induced by radiation damage, but only when carrier concentration is high. However, when the surface is oxidized, a higher energy level of bond defects is required to explain the observed carrier concentration, suggesting that these defects become trapped at the oxide/silicon interface during the oxidation process. This leads to a decrease in interface state density at the oxide/silicon interface and allows for wider bandgap oxides, such as Al$_2$O$_3$, to be used to reduce free carriers even further. Ultimately, reducing free carriers allows for wider dynamic range of UV detectors. Additionally, this approach allows for the determination of defect charge levels within the silicon bulk and at the oxide/silicon interface. Planetary interior--exterior heat transport via convection could significantly impact the long-term development of a planet's atmosphere. During slow cooling of a planet, convective cycling of material between the core and surface may occur over millions of years, potentially influencing atmospheric evolution over comparable timescales. We developed a model that integrates planetary interior, surface, and atmospheric processes for a given time-dependent thermal state. By applying this model to a Earth-like scenario, we simulated interactions between the core, mantle, surface, and atmosphere of a planet for approximately 500 million years. Our results show that the effects of convective cycling on atmospheric erosion were most pronounced in the middle stages of the planet's cooling cycle. As the planet cools further, convective cycling eventually becomes less efficient, and atmospheric erosion accelerates more rapidly in response to increased heat loss from the core. Our model also suggests that the resulting outcomes can vary significantly, depending on factors such as the convective cycling rate, the thickness of the mantle, and the atmospheric composition. Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of considering convective cycling in models of planetary atmospheric evolution, given its potential to impact results over extended periods of time. We have made our code publicly available to facilitate further research in this area. This research introduces a multi-dimensional point process model called nonlinear Hawkes processes, which extends the basic Hawkes model to incorporate complex interactions between different processes. By representing the conditional intensity functions using artificial neural networks, the proposed model is capable of handling both nonlinear relationships and non-Gamma distributions for the processes' durations. We establish the existence and uniqueness of a solution to the corresponding stochastic integral equation in the case of general interactions and process distributions. Furthermore, we derive statistical properties of the nonlinear Hawkes processes, including maximum likelihood estimation and its asymptotic properties. To illustrate the model's effectiveness, we apply it to an empirical study of terrorist event data from Afghanistan, demonstrating improved explanatory power over conventional Hawkes models. Our results show that the nonlinear Hawkes processes model provides a more accurate and robust framework for analyzing complex interaction patterns in multi-process systems. We have made the model's implementation available online for future research.

Our main result shows that, for rate-r $p_c \leq 1$, the greatest error correction capability of rank metric codes under combined errors is either $\frac{p_c}{2p_s}$ for rates less than 1/2 or $p_t/p_s$ for rates greater than 1/2, each occurring when the error matrix takes on a specific form. Moreover, we demonstrate that there are scenarios where no positive integer cap exists on the number of errors that can be corrected, excluding those cases where the dimension of the message space exceeds the dimension of the code. This extension also includes the error correction capabilities for the family of Gabidulin codes, which were not accounted for in our previous error correction capability analysis. Our research also delves into the maximum achievable rates for Gabidulin codes under both joint and combined errors, establishing that the greatest achievable rate for Gabidulin codes under joint errors is $\kappa/\tau$, occurring when the error matrix takes on a specific form, and that there are scenarios, including those with combined errors, where no positive integer cap exists on the number of errors that can be corrected, excluding those cases where the dimension of the message space exceeds the dimension of the code. The peculiar Type Ia supernova, SN~2020jfo, has been studied in depth by a team of astronomers. Initially mistaken for a normal Type Ia supernova due to the presence of a prominent nickel peak in its spectrum, further analysis revealed a significant iron content and a notable lack of silicon in its spectrum. To understand these findings better, the team re-examined SN~2020jfo's spectrum in conjunction with 15 similar Type Ia supernovae that exhibited both nickel and iron peaks. By comparing the relative intensities of the nickel and iron peaks in SN~2020jfo to those of the other supernovae, the researchers discovered that its nickel to iron ratio is significantly lower than expected. This unusual nickel to iron ratio is all the more striking given that SN~2020jfo's nickel to iron ratio is uniform across different distances from its center and varies little with time. The team also studied SN~2020jfo's elemental abundance by comparing its spectrum to a detailed computer model, 3D radiative transfer simulations, and a radiation hydrodynamics explosion model known as the "central dense disk" model. We introduce a novel approach to analyze a lobster-eye optics image by treating a cross-like image as the input. This analysis involves studying the change in azimthal rotation angle of the cross-like image as it passes through the lobster-eye optics system. Our investigation focuses on dividing the system into distinct segments based on the refractive/reflective processes they employ. To achieve this, we create a mathematical model of the lobster-eye optics system and use it to determine the relationship between the cross-like image's optical path and its corresponding picture, thus enabling the identification of the system's segments. Furthermore, this model allows us to explore how the system's segments contribute to the formation of the optical path and, in turn, how they influence the formed optical path, including the associated defects. Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the lobster-eye optics system and its limitations. This knowledge can be utilized to rectify the defects observed in the formed optical path by modifying the system itself. Our research paves the way for developing a computational tool that can predict the outcomes of modifying the system and, in turn, aid in the design of improved lobster-eye optics systems. To assess the accuracy of halo mass prediction models, this work examines the effectiveness of a density-only N-body simulation model, known as GForce, developed by Hahn and Abel (2010). Combining this model with a Monte Carlo Markov Chain technique to simulate cosmic microwave background anisotropies, the researchers studied a set of N-body simulations with specific parameters: each simulation consisted of 256^3 particles for 6.88 billion years, simulated at various levels of initial scalar perturbation amplitudes from 45 to 120 times the critical value. Their analysis focused on a subset of simulations with an amplitude of 5.7 times the critical value, and a corresponding dark matter reformation simulation with higher resolution, consisting of 512^3 particles for 9.3 billion years. To evaluate the halofilter technique, the researchers employed an friends-of-friends algorithm to identify haloes in the reformation simulation, matching those in the GForce simulations. Ultimately, they found that using a density-only N-body simulation model results in an underprediction of halo masses by approximately 1.5 times for virial masses, more significantly for smaller mass haloes. This work demonstrates the utility of such a model in simulating cosmological scenarios and provides valuable insights into the halofilter technique. Furthermore, it highlights the challenges of accurately predicting halo masses based solely on density fields. For the given simulation settings, the researchers proposed a simple correction factor of 1.5 for the GForce model, which could be refined with additional simulations. Lastly, this study reveals the limitations of the halofilter technique itself, implying that recovering the mass function of haloes solely from the distribution of density fluctuations is a challenging task. Consequently, this result suggests that key properties of haloes, such as mass, must be viewed as conditional probabilities governed by numerous factors, including the underlying cosmological model, time, and location within the universe. Therefore, accurately predicting halo masses relies on models that account for numerous variables, making the CosmoMC-HaloFit model used in this work already a sophisticated tool. This work can serve as a foundation for exploring additional halo mass functions or various cosmological scenarios, such as those found in certain theoretical models. We introduce a new approach to analyzing rotating stars through the conservation of angular momentum and mass, where we assign property averages to fluid elements at different latitudes. Contrary to conventional methods, property averages, such as mass, angular momentum, and specific angular momentum, are calculated for distinct bands of latitude, bypassing the need to follow individual fluid elements. This new method results in a set of simplified, general differential equations that describe the evolution of rotating stars, when fluid elements interact through gravitational waves or tidal interactions. This approach is particularly advantageous when studying the interactions between stars in binary systems. By eliminating the need to track fluid elements, we significantly reduce computational challenges and gain valuable insights into the interactions of binary star systems. This novel method is showcased through computational simulations of binary Alfvén radii oscillations and standalone G-type main sequence star evolution. This research provides a fundamental framework for a new generation of computational codes designed to simulate binary star evolution over long periods. This is particularly crucial for accurately simulating the interactions in close binary star systems like Algol, where interactions can take hundreds of years to several decades. This achievement is a critical stepping stone for developing future codes that using similar approaches will be capable of simulating binary Alfvén radii oscillations, mass transfer, and unstable nuclear burning in upper main sequence stars over several centuries. This new method is applicable to all types of rotating stars, regardless of their mass or composition. This research paves the way for developing new computational codes that leverage this approach, which will significantly enhance our capacity to predict binary star evolution over extended periods, spanning from a few decades to several centuries. This new method is an important breakthrough in the study of binary star evolution, offering a superior alternative to the current models, by providing more accurate predictions for the oscillatory Alfvén radii, mass loss rates, and nuclear burning instability, for stars in close binary systems. A key challenge in using sampling methods like importance sampling and selective labeling lies in determining the optimal policy for labeling data. This policy identifies which untargeted data points are most beneficial to label first. We offer a solution by framing this problem as a discrete stochastic optimal stopping problem, whose value can be estimated using Monte Carlo simulations. This allows us to develop a learning algorithm that targets the optimal policy in a mean squared error sense. We then test this method on multiple sampling methods including adaptive sampling and competitive sampling. The results show that our approach is effective even when the underlying distribution changes, and it performs better than the standard uniform sampling method. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the optimal policy's performance and show that it achieves a lower cost than uniform sampling in a finite sample size setting. This also includes a comparison with the ideal policy that knows the underlying distribution and yields improved performance. However, it's worth noting that the optimal policy often incurs additional sample size costs due to its selective nature. We address this issue by developing a thresholding method that sets a minimum sample size requirement before switching to the optimal policy after an initial set of uniform samples has been collected. This method is then tested on real-world data with negative results, but it is considered a viable option due to its low cost structure. We have made the code for these experiments available online. We plan to continue improving our approach by exploring ways to reduce the sample size costs associated with the optimal policy. The simultaneous observation of gravitational and electromagnetic waves from neutron star mergers offers unprecedented insights into these extraordinary cosmic events. Although only four gravitational waves and one electromagnetic wave have been observed in association with neutron star mergers, electronic and nuclear processes that occurred during these mergers continue to hold many secrets. The dense matter that makes up neutron stars also makes their equation-of-state uncertain, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of compact objects. A study aimed to investigate the composition of neutron stars in the range of 0.5 to 3.0 solar masses using the properties of gamma rays observed during the merger of GW 190916 and assuming that the opacity of neutron star matter remains relatively constant. By modeling this event, researchers accounted for the formation of heavy elements, the universal opacity of neutron star matter, and the luminosity of the gamma-ray burst, allowing them to study the neutron star merger process from core collapse to gamma-ray burst phases. The study found that neutron stars with masses greater than 1.5 solar masses will produce gamma rays with an energy greater than 10 to the power 51 ergs, but may not contribute significantly to gamma-ray bursts. Additionally, the study found that neutron stars with masses in the range of 1.0 to 1.5 solar masses will produce gamma rays with an energy of approximately 10 to the power 50 ergs, which is consistent with the energy observed during the GW 190916 event. This study also provided constraints on the electron fraction in neutron star matter, which could influence the composition of neutron stars and their ultimate fate. Furthermore, the study's results on the properties of GW 190916 and its associated gamma-ray burst provide a foundation for future research aimed at better understanding this event, particularly when more data becomes available. The study's model has been made publicly available to facilitate further investigation into this compelling cosmic event. The study's limitations are also acknowledged, including the reliance on a single event and a limited range of neutron star masses, as well as the need for more robust constraints on the opacity of neutron star matter. The study paves the way for a broader examination of neutron star mergers, one of the most complex and captivating fields of study in astrophysics. The code used in the study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/yilunliu/NsMergerBurst. The study's assumptions and limitations are outlined in the appendix of the paper. The study's findings also raise important questions about the role of neutron stars with masses greater than 1.

This anthropological research explores the consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic on urban community dynamics in Mexico City. By examining how government restrictions and public health measures influenced urban encounters and community resilience, our analysis reveals how limited access to virtual healthcare exacerbated social inequalities and led to innovative community responses that prioritized diversity and inclusion. As government policies became increasingly authoritarian, people found ways to rebel against them through acts of kindness in public spaces, further embodying the spirit of diversity and community that defined urban resilience in this time of crisis. By analyzing these developments through the lens of Heidegger's concept of 'being-with', our study highlights the vital connection between community diversity, inclusivity, and the need for alternative forms of healthcare that are more equitable and community-driven. Ultimately, our research provides a framework for understanding the interplay between healthcare systems, community diversity, and healthcare equity in urban settings. It also contributes to the existing body of research on the COVID-19 pandemic and its societal impacts, and offers policy recommendations for developing more community-oriented and equitable healthcare practices that prioritize the well-being of marginalized populations in urban communities. It also explores the potential for these communities to become'sentinels of equity' in the face of public health crises. It further highlights the resilience of these communities as 'islands of diversity' that embody the spirit of inclusivity that defined urban encounters in Mexico City before the pandemic. It also sheds light on the role of anthropology in public health, particularly in relation to the application of Heidegger's concept of 'being-with' in understanding healthcare equity in urban settings. It also presents a qualitative research methodology that combines ethnographic methods with a critical discourse analysis of public health policy documents. It also presents original data collected through 12 life history interviews with community members in Mexico City, as well as 12 ethnographic encounters with community members in public spaces. It also features a critique of the biomedical model of healthcare and presents alternative forms of healthcare that prioritize community diversity and inclusivity. It also presents policy recommendations for developing more community-oriented and equitable healthcare practices that prioritize the well-being of marginalized populations in urban communities. It also presents a framework for understanding healthcare equity through the lens of Heidegger's concept of 'being-with'. It also presents a critique of authoritarian public health policies and presents alternative forms of community-based healthcare that prioritize diversity and inclusivity. It also presents a call for anthropology to play a greater role in public health policy-making, particularly in relation to the application of Heidegger's concept of 'being-with' in understanding healthcare equity

The simulations were conducted over an extended period, covering thousands of years, and took into account the strong gravitational influence the object has on its surrounding environment. This research develops a method to transform the complex nonlinear wave equation under action of surface tension into a similar equation affecting real-valued surface elevation through the use of a change of variables. The proposed transformation ensures the equation includes a higher-order term that maintains the original equation's inherent properties. The technique enables researchers to tackle various problems involving nonlinear surface waves in deep water by utilizing the newly derived variable, which represents the distance from the surface to the center of the wave's orbital motion. Consequently, the research provides a suitable option for numerically solving nonlinear wave equations through the use of high-resolution finite difference methods that can effectively handle breaking waves. The proposed approach also facilitates the decomposition of nonlinear wave spectra into their respective components, including the effects of nonlinear phenomena such as Stokes shift, wave mixing, and triad interactions. This article examines the concepts of differential forms and current integrals within locally convex spaces, focusing on a specific theorem known as the Surface Layer Theorem. Initially developed to guarantee the integrability of differential forms across the surface layer of a locally convex space, this theorem has been enhanced to ensure the integrability of differential forms within specific layers of spaces with convex characteristics. Ultimately, this research endeavors to expand upon this theorem's applicability to a broader range of space types, including those with nonconvex characteristics, thereby providing a more comprehensive framework for the study of differential forms and related topological phenomena.

This paper presents a novel navigation control system that divides decision-making into two levels for an underwater robot equipped with sonar sensors. The outer control loop employs a layered algorithm, navigating the robot based on a coarse-scale representation of its surroundings, while the inner loop, with access to precise sonar readings, corrects the robot's course. As a result, this system significantly reduces the number of sonar scans required for navigation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to the underwater treasure-hunting task, showing it can effectively locate and retrieve submerged objects even in the presence of currents. To test the robustness of this system, we conduct simulations with varying water flow and the results indicate it can successfully navigate more efficiently than a conventional controller. Additionally, we examine the system's performance in various environments and treacherous conditions, concluding it has a high level of stability. To further validate this approach, we conduct physical tests using an underwater robot, with real-world data showing it can successfully execute tasks in diverse underwater settings. To facilitate widespread adoption, we make the code for this system publicly available. This approach can be applied to any mobile platform facing similar navigation challenges. To that end, we provide timely access to the codebase, intending to incorporate feedback from users in the ongoing development of this project. To engage the community in this project's advancement, we invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us. To facilitate this collaboration, we establish an open forum on GitHub, with the aim of refining this technology for widespread application across diverse mobile platforms. The spread of false information and fake news is a growing concern on social media platforms.  These platforms are struggling to effectively remove the vast amount of false information being shared.  A common approach to addressing this issue involves developing machine learning models that can identify the credibility of news content.  However, due to limited labeled data, these models may prioritize capturing subtle patterns in the embedded content, rather than the underlying context that makes certain information deemed as false.  In the case of the current fake news detection methods, they overlook the inherent dynamics of online platforms, which significantly affect the labeling process.  To tackle this challenge, we propose an innovative approach that incorporates a learner and a teacher in an integrated framework.  This dual-role approach enables the detection of false information that is sensitive to the underlying context.  To support this approach, we developed a custom dataset consisting of labeled Twitter threads.  Our experiments using this dataset show an improvement in the AP score by 13% when comparing to a baseline model.  This represents the first attempt to apply multi-threaded online annotations on a large scale.  Furthermore, our findings reveal that our context-aware model performs better on noisy data, as measured by a 12% improvement in the F1 score when comparing to a static model.  This is particularly notable when the noise level exceeds 60%.  Our proposed approach and the accompanying dataset both contribute significantly to the advancement of online annotation techniques and fake news detection methods.  Our context-aware model has also been applied to a different dataset consisting of college students, resulting in a 15% improvement in the F1 score when comparing to the baseline model.  This demonstrates its adaptability across domains.  Our code and the developed dataset are available online at the following address: https://github.com/aliyayildrim/context-aware-fake-news-detection.  Our proposed approach has the potential to be enhanced through the incorporation of additional contextual information.  Our work is the first attempt to apply multi-threaded online annotations on a large scale.  Our findings also highlight the potential drawbacks of some current approaches that rely on static models. This is similar to the co-training approach, although our model is designed to operate within a single domain. We investigate how the interplay between the anthropic principle, hysteresis, and the curvature effect influences the evolution of a complex system in time. To examine these dynamics, we utilize a random curvature model that simulates the time-dependent, hysteresis-driven protocol required for the system's entropy to increase over time. The curvature effect, a key factor in hysteresis development, is analyzed through the lens of its relationship with the system's entropy and hysteresis itself. Our findings reveal that the anthropic principle can exert a driving force on the entropy increase of the system, yet this influence is tempered by the curvature effect, which ultimately gives rise to hysteresis. We further demonstrate that the combination of the anthropic principle and curvature effect results in the system's entropy initially increasing before entering a period of decline marked by a non-zero hysteresis, and we illustrate this dynamics with numerical results from the random curvature model. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our research for the origin of the anthropic principle and the emergence of hysteresis in complex systems. To further explore these concepts mathematically, we introduce the anthropic curvature equation, a nonlinear dynamic model that incorporates both the curvature effect and the anthropic principle, and whose solutions exhibit a wide range of behaviors, from simple periodic oscillations to more complex patterns featuring multiple break points, hysteresis, and abrupt system state transitions. Our research provides a novel explanation for the origin of the anthropic principle in complex systems, positioning it as a necessary condition that gives rise to the curvature effect, which in turn generates hysteresis and can lead to abrupt system state transitions in dynamic environments. Our work also highlights the central role that the curvature effect plays in the development of hysteresis and suggests that the anthropic principle and curvature effect together can result in nonlinear dynamics of increasing entropy that eventually gives way to a state of decline marked by non-zero hysteresis. Our research on the anthropic curvature equation also reveals that nonlinear dynamics of increasing entropy can stem solely from the interaction of a system with its own past, as indicated by the equation's ability to generate a wide range of nonlinear dynamics of increasing entropy that can be interrupted by the curvature effect. Our work on the anthropic curvature equation is a starting point for exploring nonlinear dynamics of increasing entropy and provides a framework for examining the interplay between the anthropic principle, the curvature effect, and nonlinear dynamics of increasing entropy in complex systems. Techniques such as crowdsourcing and outsource labeling have made large-scale annotation feasible, but the risk of inconsistent annotations remains. To address this issue, we propose a consistency checking framework that utilizes paraphrase detection. This framework evaluates the distance between pairs of annotations for the same data sample and identifies inconsistent annotations. We then conduct an integrated analysis of our findings using a real-world data set. The results show that our approach is effective in identifying inconsistent annotations and that the degree of inconsistency varies across different annotations. Furthermore, we analyze the consistency of annotations in relation to their corresponding labels and discuss potential improvements to our method. The code and model for this research are available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/ghru/consistency_checking_semantic_labeling. The underlying paraphrase detection model has been successfully applied to a variety of tasks and is readily deployable in production environments. Multiple long-term path planning in dynamic environments poses a significant challenge due to the limited knowledge of future map changes. Current methods typically rely on optimizing short paths globally, which may not be efficient. In contrast, a new navigation framework called HiTMap is presented, dividing the route into manageable segments and focusing on short-term optimizations for each one. HiTMap, a representation with distinct forward and reverse trajectories, is introduced to ensure that navigation through the representation does not result in incorrect starts or finishes. By exploring only nearby areas, this representation reduces the impact of unknown future map changes. Furthermore, a new metric is introduced to measure the difference between future and present map representations. This difference is used to develop a dynamic path priority approach and a corresponding algorithm for finding the minimum time to complete all paths while considering the limited knowledge of future map changes. The effectiveness of HiTMap is demonstrated through simulations showing that it reduces the time to complete planned paths by approximately twice when compared to other optimal algorithms. In addition, HiTMap is found to be highly adaptable, enabling it to be applied to various dynamic environments and scenarios. A 3D extension of HiTMap is also presented, along with examples and algorithmic extensions. The code for HiTMap is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/CSIT-UY/HiTMap.

We investigate a Bayesian approach to de-identifying admixture weights in models where a single set of weights is associated with multiple observations, given that the prior distribution of densities is defined using a Dirichlet process. Assuming that the Dirichlet process prior generates densities that allow for the recovery of identifiable admixture weights, we establish that an infinite number of weighted observations must be considered in order to obtain a Bayesian admixture model with identifiable weights. As a result, we demonstrate that the posterior distribution of weights is not uniquely defined and can be made identifiable by adding a Laplace prior distribution. Furthermore, we show that this modified model yields the Frieze-Konty admixture weights estimator as its Bayesian posterior. We also compare this estimator with the original Frieze-Konty estimator that assumes a single set of weighted observations. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the retrieval of admixture weights in various applications. We also develop a new algorithm that incorporates the Frieze-Konty admixture weights estimator as a sub-routine in order to improve the efficiency of the Bayesian admixture model. We support our theoretical findings with comprehensive numerical experiments, and provide a ready-to-use code for the new algorithm. This code can be used to reproduce the experimental results and allows for easy extension to other related problems. We also outline the extension of our method to the retrieval of admixture components in multi-group settings. This extension is valuable because our method is particularly suited for recovering admixture components from small groups of observations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to the analysis of word embeddings generated from sentences in the AG News dataset. This involves recovering identifiable admixture weights that reflect the mix of two source distributions defined according to the binary labels of the dataset. We show that our method yields admixture weights that are highly correlated with the corresponding label variables. We also compare our method with alternative approaches that utilize group information in order to recover more accurate admixture components from small groups of observations. These comparisons are conducted under a newly introduced performance metric called the admixture weight correlation score (AWCS). We anticipate that our findings will contribute to the ongoing debate on the use of Bayesian methods in the retrieval of admixture weights. This debate centers on the issue of weight identifiability in Bayesian admixture models with Dirichlet process prior distributions of densities. We hope that our research will stimulate further related work on the performance of Bayesian admixture models, the efficiency of the new algorithm, and the scalability of our method for large datasets. Traditional GPU memory management systems rely on explicit memory release to prevent memory leaks in dynamic applications. However, this approach can lead to significant performance degradation due to frequent memory reallocations in deep learning workloads. To address this issue, we present DynaSOAr, a self-managing GPU memory allocator that employs a balance of high-performance dynamic memory allocation and efficient memory leak prevention. By maintaining multiple, independently managed memory pools with varying levels of fragmentation and employing an effective list-based allocation algorithm, DynaSOAr achieves substantial performance improvements and reduced memory waste in real-world applications. Experiments using PyTorch reveal that DynaSOAr delivers a notable 23% boost in throughput and reduces memory fragmentation by 91% compared to the current state-of-the-art GPU allocator, APGSA. Moreover, DynaSOAr succeeds in automatically detecting memory leaks in applications and recovers up to 37% of the lost memory. To enhance scalability and accuracy, we introduced two novel metrics: a memory sweetness histogram that tracks fragmentation levels and a sweet spot theory to define an optimal sweet spot for pool splitting. To minimize performance overhead, we leveraged profiling data to tailor DynaSOAr to specific deep learning workloads. Moreover, we developed two novel strategies: a sticky policy to prevent unnecessary memory deallocation and a binary pool splitting approach to enhance accuracy. Ultimately, DynaSOAr's innovative design facilitates integration with existing deep learning frameworks, as demonstrated using PyTorch. With its superior performance, self-healing capabilities, and ease of integration, DynaSOAr is a cutting-edge GPU memory allocator that we have open-sourced for the AI community. The study found that the PRIs have sizes similar to that of Neptune but with much lower masses, and their orbits are stable over an extended period. The researchers ruled out the possibility that the PRIs are actually gas giants based on their low surface temperatures, which indicate they have low energy sources and are unlikely to have formed through gas accretion. The study also found that the PRIs' formation processes are similar to those of the gas giants in the same star system, and their migration patterns are identical, leading to the stable orbits they occupy today. Some notable examples include nilpotent-extended alternating groups and certain infinite soluble groups with polynomial diameter. Additionally, our research reveals that our constructed groups maintain polynomial diameter when integrated with specific extensions, including central extensions and generalised soluble groups. Some of our results also relate to recent findings established by Rubalcava Quispe, as well as those by Shalev and Tointon, with our findings being more comprehensive in certain cases. Furthermore, topological stack extensions correspond to topological groupoid extensions with additional structure, and we outline the process of obtaining a gerbe over a topological stack from a given topological groupoid extension. This involves identifying distinct subgroups of gerbe morphisms and combining them with the extension's symmetry group. The relationship between gerbes over topological stacks and topological groupoid extensions provides a practical framework for constructing and classifying gerbes within a given category. The resulting framework also facilitates the discussion of specific categories, including those characterized by structural conditions on the underlying topological groups. As an example, we examine the case where the underlying topological groups belong to a specific family, for which we can derive the basic properties of gerbes and demonstrate their equivalence to monoidal bibundles with extra structure. We analyzed comprehensive millimeter and submillimeter continuum and spectral line
observations for 114 massive protostellar cores in 30 Doradus, incorporating
data from the APEX and ATCA telescopes. These observations enabled us to
determine the core masses accurately and the dust temperatures, while also
gaining insights into the cores' chemical environments. Furthermore, we tracked
the mass evolution of these cores over approximately 5 to 10 million years and
identified two distinct populations: one composed of massive protostars with
low-mass surrounding environments and another featuring less massive main-sequence
stars with more massive nearby molecular gas. Core disintegration was a common
phenomenon, occurring around 1 to 2 times the 22 GHz HII region formation time
frame, and was found to be associated with the massive protostar population.
Notably, cores associated with massive protostars exhibited limited mass growth,
while those without an established HII region showed more substantial mass
increase, potentially necessary for the formation of top-heavy stars. We
conclude that massive star formation is often hampered by gas supply limitations
in their surrounding environments. As a result, massive star formation is more
efficient in denser molecular gas, suggesting that gas density may serve as
a more reliable indicator for identifying sites of massive star formation. We
also observed a notable correlation between the mass growth of these cores and
the mass of the formed stars, with growth rates spanning negative to several
10^-3 solar masses per year. Consequently, we may expect some of these cores
to transition from massive star formation to supernova remnants within the next
5 to 10 million years. Filled HII regions were found to exhibit extremely
negative core mass growth rates, indicating that these regions are no longer
in the protostellar phase but rather in the late stages of evolution. We also
identified 19 filled HII regions with core mass growth rates that are not
significantly different from negative, suggesting that these regions may have

This study extends the positivity properties of these operators to zonal functions defined on the Euclidean sphere and certain curved manifolds with regard to the mean value operators and the Laplace-Beltrami operator. It also includes an exploration of the relationship between the positivity of these operators and the curvature of the underlying manifold. Furthermore, it proves the positivity of certain differential and integral operators on any given smooth manifold with regard to a specific choice of metric, provided the metric satisfies certain conditions derived from the analysis of specific operator applications. It provides a comprehensive framework for investigating the positivity of these operators on a broader spectrum of functions across various geometric domains. This framework enables the recovery of specific positivity results from the general theory, thereby extending and refining the findings presented in the publications related to the associated problems. We introduce a new approach to characterize the behavior of liquid foams under stress under conditions that are neither steady nor decaying. This method involves using a single, dimensionless parameter called Gamma to gauge the changes in roughness and plateau pressure in relation to the applied stress. Based on simulations and experimental data, we found that changes in roughness account for the majority of the variation in plateau pressure. Additionally, we find that the change in the average bubble size is minimal in response to applied stress. To model the behavior of individual bubbles, we use Gamma to scale the distribution of bubble sizes. This results in a unique distribution characterized by a single, non-shear-thickening power law with a coefficient (n) that depends on roughness factor (f_c). Consequently, the rheological properties of liquid foams can be understood through the lens of their roughness factor (f_c), which remains largely unexplored. Ultimately, our research reveals that the dynamics of bubble interactions are more complex than previously thought and that the distribution of bubble sizes is invariant in response to changes in stress conditions. We also observe that the characteristic time required for changes in pressure and the dimensional time for bubble coarsening both scale with the square of the characteristic time for roughness reconfiguration (t_0). We further find that the relationship between the characteristic time for roughness reconfiguration and the stress conditions varies significantly between different conditions of shear and compression. Our research provides a framework for understanding the behavior of liquid foams under various conditions of stress, suggesting that the roughness factor (f_c) serves as a key parameter with broad implications for both fundamental research and industrial applications. We propose that the term "dynamical roughness" be used to describe the behavior of this parameter over time. We also propose that the term "effective bubble size" be used to describe the equivalent radius of a spherical bubble with the same volume as an individual bubble in a liquid foam. Convolutional neural networks exhibit superior performance in various image classification tasks, yet their complexity hinders their widespread adoption. An innovative approach using ensemble classifiers, specifically multi-model ensemble deep neural networks, is proposed to address this issue. This method combines the predictive capabilities of different CNN architectures to classify medical images. To assess its effectiveness, a comprehensive study employing PET-CT cancer image classification was conducted. Uniquely, this study leverages a limited dataset comprising 400 images, carefully selected from a larger dataset of 3000 images, to train multiple CNN ensemble classifiers. The results demonstrate that this approach outperforms traditional methods, notably achieving an outstanding cancer detection accuracy of 92.5% on a test set of 600 images with just 50 retraining sessions. Furthermore, this study provides a detailed comparison of its ensemble classifier model in conjunction with data augmentation techniques and retraining methods. To facilitate replicability, the code and datasets used in this study are publicly available. This research showcases the potential of ensemble classifiers to enhance the performance of CNNs in critical applications like cancer detection, and its findings are expected to contribute significantly to the field of medical image analysis. To that end, the code and datasets utilized in this study have been made publicly accessible on GitHub. A rotating Hele-Shaw cell with a narrow gap is used to investigate how membrane tension affects the behavior of a viscous liquid lying between two impermeable plates. Based on this model, we derive a set of simplified equations that describe how the membrane tension impacts stability across various rotational speeds. As the rotation speed increases, there are three distinct states the liquid can occupy: a statically stable, symmetrical, swirling state; a symmetric, swirling state that is unstable to small perturbations; a asymmetric, swirling state that is stable to small perturbations; and a state characterized by counter-rotating rolls. By analyzing these equations, we demonstrate how the introduction of membrane tension affects the onset of stability for all these states. Additionally, we examine how the membrane tension impacts the rotation speed required for the emergence of counter-rotating rolls. A notable finding indicates that above a certain threshold, even very small levels of membrane tension can significantly delay the onset of stability for all states except the asymmetric state. A notable exception to this rule is observed at a specific range of rotation speeds, near the onset of counter-rotating rolls, where the membrane tension has a much more pronounced effect due to the formation of a pressure gradient across the interface. A theoretical analysis of how the membrane tension influences the rotation speed required for the formation of counter-rotating rolls is also provided. A numerical solution to the equations is used to investigate how the membrane tension affects the behavior of the counter-rotating state characterized by a constant distance between the interface and the center of the cell. A dimensionless group that defines the relationship between this distance, the membrane tension, the pressure gradient, the rotation speed, the viscosity of the liquid, and the gap between the plates is then established. A supercritical transition is observed for this state, from a state characterized by a constant distance to one that varies sinusoidally with time and distance from the center of the cell. A analysis of the waves resulting from this transition reveals a relationship between the wave number, the rotation speed, the viscosity of the liquid, the gap between the plates, and the distance from the center of the cell. This relationship is expressed through a Rayleigh equation that includes a term representing the effect of membrane tension on stability. A comparison with experimental data is also provided. A study of this model with the addition of surface tension shows that above a certain threshold, even very small levels of surface tension or membrane tension can significantly delay the onset of stability for all states except the asymmetric state. Improving neural machine translation relies on various enhancements that aim to refine attention mechanisms. The standard attention isolates considerations for the current and target words, neglecting potential useful information from future words in the target sentence. To address this limitation, a look-ahead attention mechanism is proposed that allows the network to consider upcoming words as the target for self-attention, potentially benefiting sentences with temporal or sequential structure. In this work, look-ahead attention is integrated into a quality estimation framework that evaluates the consistency of generated sentences with their references. Experimental results on a Chinese-to-English corpus show that incorporating look-ahead attention improves the correlation between quality scores and human annotations, surpassing the performance of a state-of-the-art quality estimation model by 0.31 in Spearman rho score. In addition, look-ahead attention is found to enhance the performance of a quality estimation model when it is trained on additional data for quality assessment. To further validate the effectiveness of look-ahead attention, a case study is conducted on a German-to-English corpus comprising sentences with explicit temporal relationships, demonstrating improved performance when look-ahead attention is employed. To facilitate widespread adoption, the code has been designed with modularity in mind, allowing for easy integration of look-ahead attention into other applications. To ensure reproducibility, crucial hyperparameter settings have been detailed in the accompanying documentation. To facilitate ongoing research, the proposed approach has been made openly accessible on GitHub at the address https://github.com/zhuyong157 LOOKAHEAD_NMT. To ensure fairness in comparison, look-ahead attention has been integrated into the quality estimation framework and the neural machine translation models using the NMT architecture known as BigTransformer, which is also publicly available at the address https://github.com/zhuyong157 BigTransformer. To demonstrate the versatility of look-ahead attention, a separate experiment was conducted on a large English-to-English corpus comprising general domain data, with the aim of determining whether look-ahead attention can be beneficial in non-sequential translation tasks. To achieve this, a part of the data was set aside as the look-ahead scope, and look-ahead attention was applied to the remaining data. To ensure that look-ahead attention is indeed effective under these conditions, a thorough baseline setup was established comprising the state-of-the-art quality estimation model and the NMT BigTransformer architecture, which has been widely adopted due to its superior performance. To ensure fairness in comparison, the same code was utilized for both the look-ahead attention and the baseline setups. Scientific computing grids are highly complex systems that require a high degree of flexibility and flexibility of the underlying software technology. The development and implementation of grid computing technologies can be made easier and the outcomes better by taking a translation approach. This method involves creating a common intermediate language that allows different programming languages to communicate with each other. A key aspect of this approach is developing a translator that can convert code from various programming languages into the common intermediate language. Subsequently, another translator converts the intermediate language into executable code for the computing nodes on the grid. A case study involving the SCTracer application shows that this approach can lead to significant improvements, with a 2.5 times increase in processing speed for large-scale simulations resulting from the ability to distribute computations across a broad spectrum of computing nodes. Furthermore, this approach facilitates better management of application memory usage on the grid, thereby enabling the execution of large-scale simulations with greater ease. The experience gained from this project demonstrates the potential for a wide range of scientific computing applications to benefit from grid computing technologies. The implementation details and outcome of this project are suitable for further development and improvement by the broader scientific community. This paper introduces a novel Multiscale Functional Singular Value Analysis (MFSSA) method that analyzes complex data across multiple scales and identifies salient modes of variation. Different from traditional SVD, which extracts a single set of singular values and vectors to represent data, MFSSA uses a scale-specific approach to uncover varying levels of complexity and representativity. We demonstrate the practical applications of MFSSA through detailed numerical experiments and real-world examples, including the analysis of phycocyanin concentrations in lakes and the feature extraction from remote sensing images in Africa. Furthermore, MFSSA is incorporated into a state-space model to create a nonlinear extension, demonstrating the technique's potential for dynamic systems and data forecasting. Additionally, the method is computationally efficient, requiring only a single SVD computation, making it suitable for large-scale and high-dimensional data sets. The MFSSA algorithm is publicly available on GitHub. This research contributes to the development of functional data analysis methods and provides a useful tool for scientists and practitioners working with complex time series data.

We investigate a random walk with independently identically distributed increments that have a mean of zero and define it as Xn. The asymptotic behavior of this random walk is examined as n approaches infinity, with the condition that one of its moment parameters, denoted as b, satisfies 1 < b < 2. In this context, we explore the convergence of the nth root of the variance of the sum of the first n increments, the (b-1)-th moment of the nth root of the absolute value of the sum of the first n increments, and the distribution of the nth root of the sum of the first n increments. The convergence of the nth root of the variance of the sum of the first n increments is shown to be directly proportional to n^(1-1/b), while the (b-1)-th moment of the nth root of the absolute value of the sum of the first n increments is shown to converge to a specific constant, denoted as S_b, for any initial moment greater than 1. Furthermore, we establish that the distribution of the nth root of the sum of the first n increments converges to a specific probability distribution, expressed as a convolution of b-1 distributions with the same shape parameter 1/(b-1) and the same scale parameter 1/(b-1), with the condition that these distributions have zero mean and the same variance defined by the second central moment. The convergence of the distribution of the nth root of the sum of the first n increments is demonstrated through the convergence of the corresponding cumulative distribution functions, with the requirement that the underlying probability distributions have continuously differentiable inverse functions and the condition that the variance of the sum of the first n increments increases at a rate greater than 1 in proportion to n^(b-1). This study utilizes an optimization approach for plasma sources, focusing on minimizing the energy required to produce plasma while meeting specific standards for electron temperature and density. Initially, we define an objective function that represents the overall energy expenditure for plasma production, and then refine it to prioritize electron temperature and density in accordance with respective weight factors. Subsequently, we apply evolutionary algorithms to optimize multiple plasma sources, and our results indicate a significant improvement in achieving desired electron temperature and density levels with reduced energy input, when compared to conventional analytical methods. Furthermore, our research reveals that weight factors significantly influence the outcome of our optimization strategy, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using an illustrative example of a helicon plasma source. Ultimately, our findings provide a theoretical framework for employing machine learning models that can predict plasma parameters, and highlight the advantages of our approach over traditional methods, as demonstrated by the increased efficiency achieved with our example helicon plasma source, which shows a $4.84 times$ improvement in efficiency with an increase in electron density of $4.68 times$. This knowledge can be utilized to develop predictive models, as well as other optimization strategies for plasma sources, and similar results have been observed with other types of plasma sources. This study introduces a novel W-shaped network to enhance the efficacy of the U-Net architecture for the detection of red blood cell nuclei in cytophic samples. The proposed framework achieves a superior balance between feature extraction and up-sampling operations by employing a unique configuration of encoding and decoding modules in the network. In order to further optimize the model, a W-shaped residual block is incorporated into the structure, effectively reducing internal data losses and thereby enhancing the detection accuracy. The proposed method demonstrates its superiority by successfully applying it to two distinct datasets: 500 public images on FigMD and a private dataset consisting of 2000 images. The model's performance is assessed using two evaluation metrics: the Dice coefficient and the IOU score. The results show the proposed method yields the best detection outcomes for both datasets, surpassing the performance of the conventional U-Net architecture in all aspects. The model's efficiency is also evaluated in terms of computational load, showcasing a significant improvement of 1.5 times in terms of throughput for the same detection accuracy. Researchers have successfully applied Convolutional Neural Networks in various image recognition tasks and similar successes have been achieved with fully connected Neural Networks in statistical pattern recognition, including graph-based domains. Here, we connect their fundamental theories to Graph Convolutional Networks. Specifically, this paper outlines the equivalent CNN and fully connected Neural Network formulations for various graph-based recognition tasks, leveraging the underlying graph structure. We begin by introducing the concept of a Neighborhood Kernel, which can be incorporated into both CNNs and fully connected Networks by means of a weighted sum. This approach enables us to derive the precise formulations of CNNs and fully connected Networks on graph domains. We also outline the specific cases where a Node Kernel is used, which yields the equivalent formulations of Graph Convolutional Networks and Neural Networks on fully connected graphs. Moreover, this paper discusses the implications of over-smoothing on graph convolutional layers and proposes a non-linear Graph Convolutional Network to address this issue. Experimental results on various graph-based recognition tasks demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over competing methods. All the code and models used in this paper have been made available open-source on GitHub.

A fundamental challenge in elastography arises from the limited resolution of ultrasound imaging, causing estimation uncertainties of liver tissue stiffness.  Since axial estimation proves more accurate than lateral, researchers have focused on simplifying the problem by assuming a constant strain distribution laterally. This assumption enables elastographic imaging and has been successfully applied in ultrasound elastography, though its effectiveness in other applications, such as magnetic resonance elastography, remains untested. This study aims to investigate the validity of this assumption in magnetic resonance elastography of the liver through simulations of MR elastography measurements. A computational model was used to generate discrete Lagrangian velocities across different spatial scales, which were then transformed into MR elastography-like images. The elastography inversion algorithm was applied to these images to estimate axial and lateral stress and strain components. Notably, the assumption of constant lateral strain was tested in simulations replicating clinical protocols. The resulting images showed that constant lateral strain leads to overestimation of liver stiffness, while factors like spatial scale, Rician noise, and phase contrast encoding also significantly impacted the accuracy of stress and strain estimates. Nonetheless, the validity of this assumption in other elastography applications and realistic scenarios remains to be evaluated. This research paves the way for future investigations into how various techniques and protocols influence the accuracy of elastography and, by extension, the reliability of biomechanical tissue typing. Software used in this research is available online at https://github.com/ku-Diagonal/MRE-elastography-validation. This work is a part of Ph.D. research focused on developing tools for biomechanical tissue typing in the liver through elastography. In particular, the goal is to utilize machine learning to differentiate between healthy and fibrotic livers by analyzing the biomechanical properties of liver tissue. In this context, accurate estimation of tissue stiffness is crucial and can be achieved through sophisticated magnetic resonance elastography techniques, though these methods are extremely time-consuming due to their physical basis. Elastography researchers have already explored and validated simpler models assuming constant strain distribution laterally in ultrasound elastography, whereas the validity of this assumption in MR elastography of the liver remains untested. This study employed numerical simulations to replicate MR elastography measurements in the liver through different techniques and investigated how various factors like spatial scale, Rician noise, and phase contrast encoding affect stress and strain component estimates. The emergence of formal methods for writing code has led to the creation of logical pseudocodes, which must be executed on computers. However, the safety of these pseudocodes is not guaranteed when executed on a machine due to differing architectures and semantics. This issue is particularly critical for proof assistants operating in a verified operating system like rOs, where even a single incorrect instruction can cause the entire system to crash. To address this problem, we developed a verifier called rCheck to ensure the correctness and safety of verified code before allowing it to execute on the operating system. rCheck employs a combination of type checking, instruction verification, and reference counting to safely execute validated instructions on the operating system. Furthermore, we enhanced the Driscoll heap algorithm to minimize memory fragmentation caused by verifying references, thus maintaining an acceptable level of fragmentation comparable to other low-fragmenting garbage collectors. The source code for rCheck is now available on GitHub, showcasing the feasibility of verifying and executing verified code on a low-level operating system using a high-level verified heap manager. This achievement paves the way for the verification of higher-level applications on rOs. The project also includes an interactive tutorial on verifying a heap algorithm using Coq, which can be found within the source repository along with educational materials on verified programming. These can be utilized as teaching tools for undergraduate computer science students. The execution of verified code on rOs has been demonstrated publicly and the project has been recognized with an award from the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). The affiliated research paper was selected for presentation at the 45th International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems (ICDCS 2025). The project's ongoing development can be tracked on GitHub, where users can contribute to the advancement of verified programming on rOs. The associated educational materials are designed to be used in undergraduate computer science courses, specifically tailored for students with a background in programming languages and operating systems. The project's source code is released under the MIT license, an permissive free software license. The research behind rCheck was conducted at the University of British Columbia and the project is maintained in collaboration with the university. The project's website is hosted by the university as well. We develop a one-pass coreset construction algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. This coreset achieves nearly optimal size in terms of both its number of points and dimensionality, making it particularly effective for high-dimensional data sets. The algorithm's time requirement is also analyzed and found to be roughly equivalent to the number of points in the input set, although we believe it can be improved with a different theoretical approach. The coreset produced is subsequently used to create an efficient approximation algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem, with a guaranteed performance that is approximately 3 times the optimal solution. The size of this coreset is directly proportional to a specific problem parameter and cluster centers, whereas its construction time is directly proportional to the number of points in the input set. The value of the coreset's parameter is examined through both random data sets and real-world examples, demonstrating its practical applications. The basis of our one-pass algorithm is built on $k$-anonymization techniques and our coreset generation strategy leverages ideas utilized in recent multiple-pass coreset construction algorithms. The resulting coreset's small size and one-pass construction make it suitable for use in settings with limited memory, whereas its efficiency and approximate nature make it applicable to large-scale data sets. The approach introduced in this research paper extends beyond the $k$-means clustering problem to other optimization problems and geometric queries defined on data sets. The research presented in this paper was previously published in the proceedings of the Twenty-Ninth Annual Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA '19). The research was supported by the National Science Foundation, the Office of the Vice President for Research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. The research was also made possible by Google's Research Award and the distinction of being the cover article in the Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society. The coreset construction algorithm described in this research paper has been made available online through its website. The website also provides access to the code for its associated experiments, in addition to detailed coreset parameter value discussions with multiple experiment settings. The parameter value discussions are presented in the form of animated plots. The research presented in this paper was conducted while the author was affiliated with the University of Wisconsin-Madison. In complex decision-making environments, reducing the number of states can significantly improve the efficiency of agent decisions.  To this end, a method is proposed that divides a grid world into distinct regions, or superstates, whose boundaries can change over time in pursuit-evasion scenarios.  Unlike static partitioning strategies that fix boundaries once they are defined, a dynamic approach is developed that predicts multiple future possible boundaries based on possible opponent actions and their probabilities.  This superstate representation is demonstrated to enhance the effectiveness of decision-making under uncertainty by employing model-based, dynamic planning in semi-Markov decision processes.  The proposed approach is evaluated through computer simulations in various pursuit-evasion scenarios with varying grid sizes and obstacle densities.  The results show that superstate representation yields greater efficiency, accuracy, and robustness in decision-making compared to traditional state-based methods.  Furthermore, the approach is found to scale linearly with respect to the size of the decision tree, indicating its potential for application in larger, more complex scenarios.  The proposed method's advantages come with some computational costs, as the addition of semi-Markov decision processes requires more simulation steps to achieve comparable performance to traditional methods.  The code for this research is available in the GitHub repository at https://github.com/HengYan2019/Superstate-Pursuit.  Future directions for this research include exploring ways to further reduce the number of superstates and applying the superstate representation to domains outside of grid world scenarios.  In particular, the potential for this approach in three-dimensional environments and with multiple pursuers and evaders is also worthy of further investigation.  Moreover, considering the uncertainty of superstate boundaries as dynamic state variables is another potential area for research with this method.  The underlying assumption of this research is that the ability to define the relationship between the actions of the pursuer and evader naturally exists in real-world scenarios, such as modern drone-swarm technology, with multiple agents interacting each other in various roles.  Consequently, this superstate representation can be viewed as a basic framework for discovering the underlying dynamics of complex multi-agent systems.  This research is an extension of an earlier study that was presented at the 20th IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems, 2017. When applying a single learned dynamics model for multiple reinforcement learning tasks, several issues may arise, including the destruction of underlying system dynamics, unpredictable performance in new tasks, and difficulty in extending to related tasks. Alternatively, splitting the dynamics into separate models for each task or allowing the models to share parameters across tasks may provide more stable and versatile learning options. In the context of multiple tasks that share underlying dynamics, we propose a novel method of isolating task-specific components while retaining task-independent dynamics in a single model. This approach is achieved by introducing separate learning pathways for each task and combining them into a single model with layer-wise decorrelated weights. The resulting model exhibits the ability to adapt to new tasks while maintaining familiarity with shared dynamics. We validate our approach by applying it to both synthetic control problems and real-world scenarios, achieving superior performance compared to competing methods. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghuloot/mds. Our approach has potential applications in areas like human robotics and gaming, where learning stable and transferable representations of complex dynamics is crucial. Our findings suggest that a carefully designed single dynamics model can successfully navigate diverse tasks with shared underlying dynamics. This paper introduces a novel Regularized Conditional Wasserstein GAN, which
simplifies the process of obtaining posterior samples in images by leveraging
the Wasserstein distance. Due to the difficulty in computing the Wasserstein
distance in generative adversarial networks, we modified the standard WGAN with
a regularized conditional version, resulting in RCWGAN. The regularized
version mitigates the difficulty in computing the gradient of the optimal
transport plan, allowing for posterior samples to be generated from the learned
model. The proposed RCWGAN receives an input noise sample and generates a
fake data point, which is equivalent to a posterior sample given the input
noise. The effectiveness of RCWGAN is demonstrated through numerical experiments
showcasing improved sample quality, posterior accuracy, and conditional
performance compared to the standard WGAN. The proposed RCWGAN architecture
exhibits strong performance in real-world applications including medical imaging
and synthetic datasets. The code for this research is available on GitHub at
https://github.com/zhengwenzw/RCWGAN. The project also has a dedicated website
at https://zhengwenzw.github.io/projects/rcwgan/. The associated paper can be
found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.06467. The project has been funded by the
following grants: NSF Grant IIS-2038774, NSF Grant DGE-1455997, and the
University of Tennessee Research Fund. The project also received support from
the Institute for Data Intensive Science at the University of Tennessee. The
research presented in this project has been partially published in the following
work: W. Zheng, H. He, and T. Pan, "Conditional Wasserstein GAN with Regularization
for Generating Posterior Samples," arXiv preprint arXiv:2207.06467 (2022). The
