We introduce a concept called "bicategorical shadows" which extends the topological Hochschild homology (THHH) to bicategorical settings, thereby connecting to the broader framework of Berman-Moss-Scholze's THH. Bicategorical shadows are defined as a natural extension of the original idea behind the HHF_1 construction. This extension allows us to derive connections between THH, HHF_1, and BTHH. Moreover, these connections enable the computation of BTHH for certain bicategories that are inherently inaccessible to THH. This is particularly evident when considering the BTHH of symmetric monoidal bicategories, for which we demonstrate that the resulting formal group is precisely the one obtained via the composition of the HHF_1 construction and the BTHH of the underlying symmetric monoidal category. This result paves the way for further exploration of the relationship between THH, HHF_1, and BTHH in the context of symmetric monoidal bicategories. This research also provides a novel interpretation of the connection between THH and HHF_1, thereby extending the original result demonstrated by Berman-Moss-Scholze to a broader range of settings. This extended version appears in the paper that first introduced the concept of bicategorical shadows. This research has been substantially expanded in the PhD thesis of the first author. To tackle the challenge of modeling complex relationships in time series data, researchers have explored the use of hyperbolic neural networks. Recent work has seen the development of hyperbolic GCNs that operate within the Lorentzian space, and these have demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional Euclidean GCNs. However, existing Lorentzian GCNs are found to be represented by an incorrect mathematical formulation, leading to suboptimal results. This paper introduces a novel Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCS) that represents the Lorentzian space correctly and provides a more efficient way to compute the graph convolution. The proposed model achieves improved performance when compared to existing solutions and is also computationally more efficient. When applied to both skew-symmetric and non-skew-symmetric adjacency matrices, LGCS demonstrates its versatility. To validate the model's performance, extensive experiments are conducted on both real-world datasets and a synthetic dataset, showing its performance superiority over the current state-of-the-art hyperbolic GCNs. This includes the Lorentzian GCN, SAGCN, and PAGCN, and a baseline Euclidean GCN. The proposed LGCS is found to achieve the highest performance on seven out of ten experiments conducted. This confirms the model's effectiveness and provides a more accurate representation of graph convolution operations within the Lorentzian space. This representation is found to be critical for accurately representing complex geometric relationships in time series data, leading to a significant improvement of 2.43% in average F1-score compared to the current state-of-the-art hyperbolic GCNs. This makes LGCS a valuable contribution to the field of graph convolution networks operating within the Lorentzian space. This achievement is made possible by the model's ability to accurately capture long-distance temporal relationships by enhancing the graph convolution operation within the Lorentzian space. This enables the model to effectively learn from both local and distant data points, thereby boosting its performance. This is further validated by the model's ability to achieve the highest average F1-score of 96.58% on the MIMII-large dataset, which is a challenging dataset that is commonly used to evaluate the effectiveness of hyperbolic neural networks. This represents a significant improvement of 2.43% over the current state-of-the-art hyperbolic GCNs. This confirms the model's capability to handle complex temporal relationships in time series data and its potential to be applied in various real-world scenarios. This is demonstrated by the model's application in a real-world scenario

This investigation involves analyzing the inclusion of a mass term in the linearized Einstein-Hilbert action through various degrees of freedom in the theory. By exploring the inclusion of a mass term for the trace of the metric, a mass term for a specific combination of the $l=2$ sector's degrees of freedom, and a mass term that is universally applied across all degrees of freedom, we uncover both desirable and problematic aspects of this approach. While a mass term can eliminate unwanted degrees of freedom and modify the behavior of others, it also introduces an undesirable massive mode that becomes ghostly under a specific value of the de Sitter space's Hubble constant, $H^2=2m^2$. dynamics for each of these state types, and in the process, we derive relevant 
formulas for the corresponding Hamiltonian operators. Ultimately, our study 
provides a Hamiltonian framework for studying quantum equilibrium states in 
contact Hamiltonian dynamics. 
We also explore the relationship between these dynamics and the extensive 
quantum observables, finding that they give rise to the associated Hamiltonian 
operators when applied to the quantum equilibrium state's associated total 
energy. This connection allows us to define four distinct categories of 
Hamiltonian operators, each corresponding to a specific dynamics. These operators 
can be identified within an operator's own dynamics, as well as within the 
dynamics of the quantum system's environment. Consequently, our work paves the 
way for examining energy conservation within the context of these dynamics. 
Notably, our findings also highlight the inherent link between the Hamiltonian 
operators and the quantum equilibrium state's associated total energy, an 
energetic quantity that is itself invariant under the mentioned dynamics. 
Our study in this paper lays the groundwork for exploring quantum equilibrium 
states within the context of contact Hamiltonian dynamics, with a specific 
emphasis on the conservation of energy. 
With our new Hamiltonian framework in place, we are able to investigate the 
conservation of energy for each of the four dynamics mentioned above.

A key aspect of transition metal oxides that exhibit unconventional electronic behavior is the strong spin-orbit coupling. However, due to interactions with other electrons in salient orbital states, the effective spin-orbit coupling can be modified by the kind of crystal field present. Theoretical studies have made various predictions based on narrow orbital states, but there is a lack of predictive models that account for the large orbital components common in many 3d transition metal oxides. The focus of this study is on developing a relevant spin-orbit coupling parameter for the hub of an atomic moment within insulating transition metal oxides, going beyond the effective spin-orbit coupling in the Hubbard model by incorporating both on-site and nearest-neighbor crystal field effects. The resulting spin-orbit coupling parameter shows minimal site dependence within cuprates and tapecites, allowing for a more universal description of their electronic behavior. The parameter in question was found to influence various electronic phase diagrams of these materials, enabling the prediction of possible phase transitions in rare earth transition metal oxides. The connection between rare earth element substitution, spin-orbit coupling, crystal field, and possible phase transitions in these oxides has been established, offering a theoretical explanation for the limited site dependence of rare earth elements in transition metal oxides and providing a means to predict suitable elements for desired phases of matter. The scope of this study can be expanded to other classes of materials, like rare earth transition metal alloys and dichalcogenides, with tailored spin-orbit coupling for exotic electronic phases. These functions possess certain properties, specifically relating to relative $I$-functions on toric complete intersections with smooth divisors within their normal crossings loci. We demonstrate that the relative $I$-functions for these intersections are interconnected by means of relative $I$-functions associated with integral transforms. Moreover, when the context involves multiple intersections, we can derive relationships between the relative $I$-functions for each intersection. This leads to an integral representation of the relative $I$-functions for each toric complete intersection. This representation can be further interpreted as a kind of superabundant series, offering an alternative to the conventional definition of relative $I$-functions for integral transforms. This alternative allows us to extend the domain of relative $I$-functions to include the singular locations within the context's normal crossings locus. As a result, we can investigate relative $I$-functions for toric complete intersections near their singular divisor components. This analysis provides us with formulas for the relative $I$-functions in this specific setting. Furthermore, we discover connections between these functions and the irreducible components of the singular divisors. This discovery enables us to determine the structure of the singularities for any given toric complete intersection. This determination is equivalent to classifying the normal form for germs of complex hypersurface singularities based on their mixed Hodge modules. This classification arises from the relative $I$-functions' association with the mixed Hodge module's structure, resulting from the combination of the local monodromy and the mixed Hodge module of the hypersurface's singularities. This connection allows us to employ the relative $I$-functions to compute specific invariants of the singularities' mixed Hodge modules. Consequently, we can calculate the rank and the pole numbers of the combined local monodromy and the mixed Hodge module of the singularities. Additionally, we establish relationships between these invariants and the relative $I$-functions. To explore the potential of generative models in enhancing the quality of medical image analysis, this work investigates how altering latent codes affects the representation of tumors in tumors versus non-tumor images. By examining the effects of code modifications on different aspects of the model, our research finds that tumors and non-tumors are represented separately in the latent space, with the model ignoring superfluous information. To validate this finding, we train a model to identify the presence of tumors from the latent codes, and the results show that this model performs better when the code represents only tumors or non-tumors, rather than both. Consequently, this implies that the model is not benefiting from the presence of both tumors and non-tumors in the training data for the same sample. This finding is further confirmed by analyzing the similarity between tumors and code-mixed samples, showing that the model treats tumors and non-tumors as distinct entities in the latent space. To simplify the problem, we propose a new task that involves classifying synthetic code-mixed samples as representing tumors or non-tumors. This research was conducted using MRI scans of the liver. This work was published in the year 2023. It is worth noting that the approach discussed here is the first to examine the ability of a model to detect tumors from altered latent codes. This discovery has significant implications for future research aimed at leveraging generative models to enhance medical image analysis. To facilitate this progress, we suggest developing methods that are capable of manipulating latent codes to analyze lesions in medical images. This can be achieved by exploring code manipulation in the context of medical images that represent healthy and diseased tissue simultaneously. This research provides a starting point for this exciting area of study. In contrast, ViDaExpert strives to strike a balance between high image quality and low dimensional representation, achieving this balance through a novel use of attention mechanisms in a decoder-based architecture. ViDaExpert's attention mechanism's tailored application enables it to automatically identify crucial features in high-dimensional spaces, effectively simplifying complex data.
